Early studies found that between 24% and 40% of participating families of police officers reported incidents of domestic violence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Neidig |first1=Peter H. |title=Interspousal Aggression in Law Enforcement Families: A Preliminary Investigation |journal=Police Studies: The International Review of Police Development |date=1992 |volume=15 |issue=30 |pages=30–38 |url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/LandingPage?handle=hein.journals/polic15&div=12&id=&page= |access-date=6 October 2019 |archive-date=7 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200507074537/https://heinonline.org/HOL/LandingPage?handle=hein.journals%2Fpolic15&div=12&id=&page= |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=L. |title=On the front lines: police stress and family well-being. |date=20 May 1991 |pages=32–48 |publisher=Government Printing Office}}, Hearing Before the Select Committee on Children, Youth, and Families, U.S. House of Representatives, 102 Congress, First Session</ref> Subsequent studies suggested possible rates of officer-involved domestic violence that ranged from 4.8% to 28%,<ref name=pappas>{{cite journal |last1=Russell |first1=Brenda L |last2=Pappas |first2=Nicholas |title=Officer involved domestic violence |journal=International Journal of Police Science & Management |date=11 June 2018 |volume=20 |issue=2 |page=135 |doi=10.1177/1461355718774579|s2cid=150327201 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mennicke |first1=Annelise M. |last2=Ropes |first2=Katie |title=Estimating the rate of domestic violence perpetrated by law enforcement officers: A review of methods and estimates |journal=Aggression and Violent Behavior |date=November 2016 |volume=31 |pages=157–164 |doi=10.1016/j.avb.2016.09.003}}</ref> meaning the rate could be the same as that of the general public.<ref name=pappas /> The prevalence of domestic violence in law enforcement is important, as police attitudes toward domestic violence affect the quality of police intervention in domestic violence situations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McPhedran |first1=Samara |last2=Gover |first2=Angela R. |author3=[[Paul Mazerolle]] |title=A cross-national comparison of police attitudes about domestic violence: a focus on gender |journal=Policing: An International Journal of Police Strategies & Management |date=15 May 2017 |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=214–227 |doi=10.1108/PIJPSM-06-2016-0083|hdl=10072/338490 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Amalia R. |last2=Segal |first2=Carmit |date=2013 |title=Do Female Officers Improve Law Enforcement Quality? Effects on Crime Reporting and Domestic Violence Escalation |url=http://www.ubscenter.uzh.ch/assets/workingpapers/WP9_Do_Female_Officers_Improve_Law_Enforcement_Quality.pdf |url-status=live |journal=UBS Center Working Paper Series Working Paper |issue=9 |doi=10.2139/ssrn.2335990 |s2cid=3281431 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430210200/https://www.ubscenter.uzh.ch/assets/workingpapers/WP9_Do_Female_Officers_Improve_Law_Enforcement_Quality.pdf |archive-date=2019-04-30 |access-date=2019-12-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Police Family Violence Fact Sheet |url=http://womenandpolicing.com/violenceFS.asp |website=National Center for Women & Policing |publisher=Feminist Majority Foundation |access-date=6 October 2019 |archive-date=5 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191005000834/http://womenandpolicing.com/violenceFS.asp |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Gender aspects of abuse===
{{See also|Domestic violence#Gender differences}}
According to the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)]], in 2022 individuals identifying as women and men reported intimate partner violence around 41% and 26%, respectively, in the United States.<ref name=Fast_Facts>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-23 |title=Fast Facts: Preventing Intimate Partner Violence {{!}}Violence Prevention{{!}}Injury Center{{!}}CDC |access-date=2024-03-31 |website=www.cdc.gov |url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/intimatepartnerviolence/fastfact.html}}</ref> The [[National Crime Victimization Survey]] (NCVS) indicates that in 1998 about 876,340 violent crimes were committed in the U.S. against women by their current or former spouses, or boyfriends.<ref>{{cite web | last1 = Maleque | first1 = Saqi S. | last2 = Brennan | first2 = Virginia |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120219231718/http://www.mmc.edu/www.meharry.org/Fl/Women%27s_Health/Domestic_Violence.html |archive-date = 19 February 2012 |website = meharry.org |publisher = [[Meharry Medical College]] |url=http://www.mmc.edu/www.meharry.org/Fl/Women%27s_Health/Domestic_Violence.html   |title=Domestic violence}}</ref> According to the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]], in the United States 41% of women and 26% of men experience intimate partner violence in their lifetime, under "contact sexual violence, physical violence, and/or stalking".<ref name=Fast_Facts />

Research reviews have concluded that women's physical violence against men is more likely to be caused by self-defense and/or retaliation.<ref name="Swan">{{Cite journal|last1=Swan|first1=Suzanne C.|last2=Gambone|first2=Laura J.|last3=Caldwell|first3=Jennifer E.|last4=Sullivan|first4=Tami P.|last5=Snow|first5=David L.|date=2008|title=A Review of Research on Women's Use of Violence With Male Intimate Partners |journal=Violence and Victims|volume=23|issue=3|pages=301–314 |pmc=2968709|pmid=18624096|doi=10.1891/0886-6708.23.3.301}}</ref><ref name="Merritt">{{Cite journal|last1=Bair-Merritt|first1=Megan H|last2=Crowne|first2=Sarah Shea|last3=Thompson|first3=Darcy A|last4=Sibinga|first4=Erica|last5=Trent|first5=Maria|last6=Campbell|first6=Jacquelyn|date=October 2010|title=Why Do Women Use Intimate Partner Violence? A Systematic Review of Women's Motivations|journal=Trauma, Violence & Abuse|volume=11|issue=4|pages=178–189|doi=10.1177/1524838010379003|issn=1524-8380|pmc=2994556|pmid=20823071}}</ref> A 2010 [[systematic review]] of the literature on women's perpetration of IPV found that anger, [[self-defense]] and retaliation were common motivations but that distinguishing between self-defense and retaliation was difficult.<ref name="Merritt"/>

With regard to similar rates and a difference in methods, a study compiled by Martin S. Fiebert, suggested that women are as likely to be violent to men, but that men are less likely to be hurt. He, however, stated that men are seriously injured in 38 percent of the cases in which "extreme aggression" is used. Fiebert additionally stated that his work was not meant to minimize the serious effects of men who abuse women.<ref name="Fiebert">{{cite web |last=Fiebert |first=Martin S. |date=June 2012 |title=References examining assaults by women on their spouses or male partners: an annotated bibliography |url=http://www.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/assault.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210713122735/https://web.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/assault.htm |archive-date=13 July 2021 |access-date=23 December 2011 |website=csulb.edu |publisher=[[California State University, Long Beach]] |quote=This bibliography examines 282 scholarly investigations: 218 empirical studies and 64 reviews and/or analyses, which demonstrate that women are as physically aggressive, or more aggressive, than men in their relationships with their spouses or male partners. The aggregate sample size in the reviewed studies exceeds 369,800.}}

* ''First published as'': {{Cite journal |last=Fiebert |first=Martin S. |date=1997 |title=References examining assaults by women on their spouses or male partners: an annotated bibliography |url=https://link.springer.com/journal/volumesAndIssues/12119 |url-status=live |journal=Sexuality and Culture |volume=1 |pages=273–286 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026002348/https://link.springer.com/journal/volumesAndIssues/12119 |archive-date=2017-10-26 |access-date=2017-10-25}}
* ''Second version published as'': {{Cite journal |last=Fiebert |first=Martin S. |date=June 2004 |title=References examining assaults by women on their spouses or male partners: an annotated bibliography |journal=Sexuality and Culture |volume=8 |issue=3–4 |pages=140–176 |doi=10.1007/s12119-004-1001-6 |s2cid=195302233}}
* ''Third version published as'': {{Cite journal |last=Fiebert |first=Martin S. |date=March 2010 |title=References examining assaults by women on their spouses or male partners: an annotated bibliography |journal=Sexuality and Culture |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=49–91 |doi=10.1007/s12119-009-9059-9 |s2cid=2850888}}
* ''Fourth version published as'': {{Cite journal |last=Fiebert |first=Martin S. |date=June 2014 |title=References examining assaults by women on their spouses or male partners: an annotated bibliography |journal=Sexuality and Culture |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=405–467 |doi=10.1007/s12119-013-9194-1 |s2cid=14991601}} Available to download as a word document [http://www.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/assaults_bib343_201307.doc here.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141117065714/http://www.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/assaults_bib343_201307.doc|date=2014-11-17}}</ref><ref name=csulb>{{cite news | last = Parsons | first = Dana | title = Pitcher's case throws a curve at common beliefs about abuse | url = http://www.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/latimes.htm | work = [[Los Angeles Times]] | location = Orange County | date = 10 April 2002 | access-date = 18 November 2011 | archive-date = 22 December 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111222052031/http://www.csulb.edu/~mfiebert/latimes.htm | url-status = live }}</ref>{{#tag:ref|Martin S. Fiebert of the Department of Psychology at [[California State University, Long Beach]], has compiled an annotated bibliography of research relating to spousal abuse by women on men. This bibliography examines 275 scholarly investigations: 214 empirical studies and 61 reviews and/or analyses appear to demonstrate that women are as physically aggressive, or more aggressive, than men in their relationships with their spouses or male partners. The aggregate sample size in the reviewed studies exceeds 365,000.<ref name=Fiebert/> In a ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' article about male victims of domestic violence, Fiebert suggests that "...consensus in the field is that women are as likely as men to strike their partner but that—as expected—women are more likely to be injured than men."<ref name=csulb/>|group=nb}} A 2011 review by researcher Chan Ko Ling from the [[University of Hong Kong]] found that perpetration of minor partner violence was equal for both men and women but more severe partner violence was far likelier to be perpetrated by men.<ref name=chan2011 /> His analysis found that men were more likely to beat up, choke or strangle their partners while women were more likely to throw objects, slap, kick, bite, punch, or hit with an object.<ref name=chan2011>{{Cite journal | last = Chan | first = Ko Ling | title = Gender differences in self-reports of intimate partner violence: a review | journal = [[Aggression and Violent Behavior]] | volume = 16 | issue = 2 | pages = 167–175 | doi = 10.1016/j.avb.2011.02.008 | date = March–April 2011 | url = http://hub.hku.hk/bitstream/10722/134467/1/Content.pdf | url-status = live | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151208161311/http://hub.hku.hk/bitstream/10722/134467/1/Content.pdf | archive-date = 2015-12-08 | hdl = 10722/134467 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> The [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] also reported that women are far more likely to use objects.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Greenfield | first1 = Lawrence A. | title = Violence by intimates: analysis of data on crimes by current or former spouses, boyfriends, and girlfriends | journal = [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] | date = March 1998 | url = https://www.ncjrs.gov/App/Publications/abstract.aspx?ID=167237 | display-authors = etal | access-date = 2015-12-03 | archive-date = 2022-05-20 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220520171147/https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/violence-intimates-analysis-data-crimes-current-or-former-spouses | url-status = live }} {{ncj|167237}} [http://bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/vi.pdf Pdf.]</ref> The [[National Institute of Justice]] contends that national surveys supported by NIJ, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Bureau of Justice Statistics that examine more serious assaults do not support the conclusion of similar rates of male and female spousal assaults. These surveys are conducted within a safety or crime context and find more partner abuse by men against women.<ref name="ojp.usdoj.gov">{{cite web | title = Measuring intimate partner (domestic) violence | url = http://www.nij.gov/topics/crime/intimate-partner-violence/pages/measuring.aspx | website = nij.gov | publisher = [[National Institute of Justice]] | date = 12 May 2010 | access-date = 3 December 2015 | archive-date = 20 May 2022 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220520171150/https://nij.ojp.gov/topics/articles/overview-intimate-partner-violence | url-status = live }}</ref>{{#tag:ref|The [[National Institute of Justice]] states that studies finding equal or greater frequency of abuse by women against men are based on data compiled through the [[Conflict Tactics Scale]]. This survey tool was developed in the 1970s and may not be appropriate for intimate partner violence research because it does not measure control, coercion, or the motives for conflict tactics; it also leaves out sexual assault and violence by ex-spouses or partners and does not determine who initiated the violence.<ref name="ojp.usdoj.gov"/>|group=nb}}

[[Murray A. Straus|Straus]] and [[Richard James Gelles|Gelles]] found that in couples reporting spousal violence, 27 percent of the time the man struck the first blow; in 24 percent of cases, the woman initiated the violence. The rest of the time, the violence was mutual, with both partners brawling. The results were the same even when the most severe episodes of violence were analyzed. In order to counteract claims that the reporting data was skewed, female-only surveys were conducted, asking females to self-report, and the data was the same.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Straus | first1 = Murray A. | last2 = Gelles | first2 = Richard J. | author-link1 = Murray A. Straus | contribution = How violent are American families? Estimates from the national family violence resurvey and other studies | editor-last1 = Straus | editor-first1 = Murray A. | editor-last2 = Gelles | editor-first2 = Richard J. | others = Christine Smith (contributor) | editor-link1 = Murray A. Straus | title = Physical violence in American families: risk factors and adaptations to violence in 8,145 families | page = [https://archive.org/details/physicalviolence0000stra/page/105 105] | publisher = Transaction Publishers | location = New Brunswick, New Jersey | year = 1990 | isbn = 9780887382635 | postscript = . | url = https://archive.org/details/physicalviolence0000stra/page/105 }}</ref> The simple tally of physical acts is typically found to be similar in those studies that examine both directions, but studies show that male violence is more serious. Male violence does more damage than female violence;<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Vivian | first1 = Dina | last2 = Langhinrichsen-Rohling | first2 = Jennifer | title = Are bi-directionality violent couples mutually victimized? A gender-sensitive comparison | journal = [[Violence & Victims]] | volume = 9 | issue = 2 | pages = 107–124 | pmid = 7696192 | date = Summer 1994 | doi = 10.1891/0886-6708.9.2.107 | s2cid = 19704861 }}</ref> women are more likely to be injured and/or hospitalized. Women are more likely to be killed by an intimate than the reverse (according to the Department of Justice, the rate is 63.7% to 36.3%),<ref>{{citation | last1 = Cooper | first1 = Alexia | last2 = Smith | first2 = Erica L. | contribution = The sex distribution of homicide victims and offenders differed by type of homicide | editor-last1 = Cooper | editor-first1 = Alexia | editor-last2 = Smith | editor-first2 = Erica L. | title = Homicide trends in the United States, 1980-2008 | page = 10 | publisher = [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]], [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] | date = November 2011 | url = https://www.ncjrs.gov/app/publications/abstract.aspx?id=258006 | postscript = . }} {{ncj|236018}} [http://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/htus8008.pdf Pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180415042235/https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/htus8008.pdf |date=2018-04-15 }}</ref> and women in general are more likely to be killed by their spouses than by all other types of assailants combined.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Browne | first1 = Angela | last2 = Williams | first2 = Kirk R. | title = Exploring the effect of resource availability and the likelihood of female-perpetrated homicides | journal = [[Law and Society Review]] | volume = 23 | issue = 1 | pages = 75–94 | doi = 10.2307/3053881 | date = 1989 | jstor = 3053881 }}</ref>

Studies have found that men are much less likely to report victimization in these situations.<ref name=Gender07>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eXoPnQwEnmoC&pg=PA5|title=Family Interventions in Domestic Violence: A Handbook of Gender-Inclusive Theory and Treatment|first1=John Hamel|last1=LCSW|first2=Tonia L. Nicholls|last2=PhD|date=September 26, 2006|publisher=Springer Publishing Company|isbn=978-0-8261-0329-1 |via=Google Books}}</ref> According to some studies, less than 1% of domestic violence cases are reported to the police.<ref name=Roberts2007>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPuU1KxEORwC|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407160819/https://books.google.com/books?id=gPuU1KxEORwC&source=gbs_ViewAPI&printsec=frontcover&redir_esc=y|url-status=dead|title=Social Work in Juvenile and Criminal Justice Settings|first1=Albert R.|last1=Roberts|first2=David W.|last2=Springer|date=June 23, 2007|archivedate=April 7, 2022|publisher=Charles C Thomas Publisher| isbn=978-0-398-07676-4 |via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Sigler | first = Robert T. | title = Domestic violence in context: an assessment of community attitudes | publisher = Lexington Books | location = Lexington, Massachusetts | year = 1989 | isbn = 9780669209365 | url = https://archive.org/details/domesticviolence0000sigl }}</ref> In the United States 10–35% of the population will be physically aggressive towards a partner at some point in their lives.<ref name=Fiebert/><ref name=straus>{{citation | last = Straus | first = Murray A. | author-link = Murray A. Straus | contribution = The controversy over domestic violence by women: a methodological, theoretical, and sociology of science analysis | editor-last1 = Arriaga | editor-first1 = Ximena B. | editor-last2 = Oskamp | editor-first2 = Stuart | title = Violence in intimate relationships | pages = 17–44 | publisher = Sage Publications | location = Thousand Oaks, California | year = 1999 | isbn = 9780761916437 | postscript = .}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last = Archer | first = John | title = Sex differences in aggression between heterosexual partners: a meta-analytic review | journal = [[Psychological Bulletin]] | volume = 126 | issue = 5 | pages = 651–680 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.126.5.651 | pmid = 10989615 | date = September 2000 | quote = Meta-analyses of sex differences in physical aggression to heterosexual partners and in its physical consequences are reported. Women were slightly more likely (d = –.05) than men to use one or more acts of physical aggression and to use such acts more frequently. Men were more likely (d = .15) to inflict an injury, and overall, 62% of those injured by a partner were women. }} [http://www.batteredmen.com/ArcherSexDifferencesMeta-AnalyticReviewf2000.pdf Pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170317164606/http://batteredmen.com/ArcherSexDifferencesMeta-AnalyticReviewf2000.pdf |date=2017-03-17 }}
* {{Cite journal | last = Frieze | first = Irene | title = Violence in close relationships—development of a research area: Comment on Archer | journal = [[Psychological Bulletin]] | volume = 126 | issue = 5 | pages = 681–684 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.126.5.681 | pmid = 10989616 | date = September 2000 | quote = Assumptions of and conclusions made by feminist researchers about the problems of battered wives are reviewed. It is argued that their focus on marital violence as a form of aggression against women by men and their concern for severely beaten wives may have caused them to ignore high levels of female violence in marriage and dating. J. Archer's meta-analysis of studies of marital and dating violence showed that both sexes display violence in these relationships, although women are more likely to be injured. }}
* {{Cite journal | last = O'Leary | first = K. Daniel | title = Are women really more aggressive than men in intimate relationships? Comment on Archer | journal = [[Psychological Bulletin]] | volume = 126 | issue = 5 | pages = 685–689 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.126.5.685 | pmid = 10989617 | date = September 2000 | quote = J. Archer's conclusion that women engage in slightly more physical aggression than men in intimate relationships but sustain more injuries is reasonable in representative samples. }}</ref> As abuse becomes more severe women become increasingly overrepresented as victims.<ref name=straus/> The ''National Violence Against Women Survey'' for 2000 reported that 25% of women and 7.6% of men reported being victims of intimate partner violence at some point in their lives.<ref name=autogenerated3>{{cite book | last = WHO | author-link = World Health Organization | title = Violence against women and HIV/AIDS: critical intersections: intimate partner violence and HIV/AIDS. The global coalition on women and AIDS | url = http://www.cabsa.org.za/content/violence-against-women-and-hivaids-critical-intersections | publisher = [[World Health Organization]] | access-date = 11 April 2014 | archive-date = 8 December 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151208065252/http://www.cabsa.org.za/content/violence-against-women-and-hivaids-critical-intersections | url-status = dead }} Information Bulletin Series, Number 1. [https://www.who.int/hac/techguidance/pht/InfoBulletinIntimatePartnerViolenceFinal.pdf Pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131025220637/http://www.who.int/hac/techguidance/pht/InfoBulletinIntimatePartnerViolenceFinal.pdf |date=2013-10-25 }}</ref> The rate of intimate partner violence in the U.S. declined from 1993 until 2014, after which the number of women killed by an intimate partner began to rise while the number of men killed by an intimate partner continued to decline.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Intimate Partner Violence in the U.S.: overview: intimate partner violence has been declining | journal = [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] | archive-date = 11 December 2009 | url = http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/intimate/overview.htm | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091211222328/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/intimate/overview.htm }}</ref><ref name="fridel">{{cite journal |last1=Fridel |first1=Emma E. |last2=Fox |first2=James Alan |title=Gender Differences in Patterns and Trends in U.S. Homicide, 1976–2017 |journal=Violence and Gender |date=March 2019 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=27–36 |doi=10.1089/vio.2019.0005|s2cid=150775576 }}</ref>

In a 2006 Amnesty International report, ''The Maze of Injustice: The Failure to Protect Indigenous Women From Sexual Violence in the USA'',<ref>{{cite book | last = AI USA | author-link = Amnesty International USA | title = Maze of injustice: the failure to protect indigenous women from sexual violence in the USA | publisher = [[Amnesty International USA]] | location = New York | year = 2007 | url = http://www.amnestyusa.org/our-work/issues/women-s-rights/violence-against-women/maze-of-injustice | id = AMR 35/057/2007 | isbn = 9781887204477 | access-date = 2015-12-03 | archive-date = 2015-12-08 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151208105325/http://www.amnestyusa.org/our-work/issues/women-s-rights/violence-against-women/maze-of-injustice | url-status = live }} [http://www.amnestyusa.org/pdfs/mazeofinjustice.pdf English pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180724015602/https://www.amnestyusa.org/pdfs/mazeofinjustice.pdf |date=2018-07-24 }} [https://www.amnesty.org/download/Documents/60000/amr510352007fra.pdf French pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208081251/https://www.amnesty.org/download/Documents/60000/amr510352007fra.pdf |date=2015-12-08 }} [https://www.amnesty.org/download/Documents/60000/amr510352007es.pdf Spanish pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208075716/https://www.amnesty.org/download/Documents/60000/amr510352007es.pdf |date=2015-12-08 }}</ref> the data for Native women indicates high levels of sexual violence. Statistics gathered by the U.S. government reveal that Native American and Alaska Native women are more than 2.5 times more likely to be sexual assaulted than women in the United States in general;<ref>{{cite journal | last = Perry | first = Steven W. | title = A BJS statistical profile, 1992-2002: American Indians and crime | journal = [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] | date = December 2004 | url = http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=386 | access-date = 2015-12-03 | archive-date = 2022-05-20 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220520171148/https://bjs.ojp.gov/library/publications/american-indians-and-crime-bjs-statistical-profile-1992-2002 | url-status = live }} [http://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/aic02.pdf Pdf.]</ref> more than one in three Native women will be raped in their lifetime.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Tjaden | first1 = Patricia | last2 = Thoennes | first2 = Nancy | title = Full report of the prevalence, incidence, and consequences of violence against women: findings from the national violence against women survey | publisher = [[National Institute of Justice]] and the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] | date = November 2000 | url = http://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21948 | access-date = 2015-12-03 | archive-date = 2015-12-08 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151208164841/http://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21948 | url-status = live }} {{ncj|183781}} [https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/183781.pdf Pdf.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181120225742/https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/183781.pdf |date=2018-11-20 }}</ref>

===Statistics===
====Over the past few decades====
* In 1995–96, a UN national study found that 1% of all women participants (over 18, with or without partners or spouses) had been victims of domestic abuse within the previous 12-month period. Since this population included women who had never been partnered, the prevalence of domestic violence may have been greater among partnered women.<ref name=UN54>[https://www.un.org/ga/search/view_doc.asp?symbol=A/61/122/Add.1 ''In-depth study on all forms of violence against women.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131129135804/http://www.un.org/ga/search/view_doc.asp?symbol=A%2F61%2F122%2FAdd.1 |date=2013-11-29 }} United Nations, General Assembly. 6 July 2006. Page 54. Retrieved 16 November 2011.</ref>
* In 2000, a report by the [[United States Department of Justice]] found that 1.3% of women and 0.9% of men reported experiencing domestic violence in the past year.<ref name=Tjaden/>
* About 2.3 million people are raped or physically assaulted each year by a current or former intimate partner or spouse.<ref name=VAWA2005>[http://nnedv.org/docs/Policy/VAWA2005FactSheet.pdf ''The Violence Against Women Act of 2005, Summary of Provisions.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111216044215/http://nnedv.org/docs/Policy/VAWA2005FactSheet.pdf |date=2011-12-16 }} National Network to End Domestic Violence. Retrieved 2011-11-20.</ref>
* Physically assaulted women receive an average of 6.9 physical assaults by the same partner per year.<ref name=VAWA2005/>
* In 2019, a study found that the number of women murdered by an intimate partner had increased to an average of almost four per day. It reflected a gradual rise in the figures since 2014 after a steady reduction over the previous 40 years.<ref name="fridel" /> Focusing just on gun-related deaths, it was reported in 2019 that 50 American women per month were shot and killed by intimate partners.<ref>{{cite book |last=Snyder |first=Rachel Louise |title=No Visible Bruises: What We Don't Know About Domestic Violence Can Kill Us |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |year=2019 |page=272 |isbn=978-1635570977}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Roth |first=Alisa |title=An Epidemic of Violence We Never Discuss |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/07/books/review/rachel-louise-snyder-no-visible-bruises.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=June 7, 2019}}</ref>
* Female victimization rates may vary by race or ethnicity, as [[White American|white women]] and [[African American|black women]] were more likely to be victims of beatings than were [[Asian Americans|Asian]] or [[Hispanic Americans|Hispanic women]], according to a 2012 study.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Karmen |first1=Andrew |title=Crime Victims: An Introduction to Victimology |date=13 April 2015 |publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=978-1-305-46549-7 |page=298 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jjh-BAAAQBAJ&dq=women+crime+risk&pg=PA298 }} "African-American women faced higher risks, and Hispanic and Asian women faced lower risks of beatings than white women in 2010 (Catalano, 2013)."</ref>

* A mid‑year report from the [[Council on Criminal Justice]] (CCJ), which monitors crime trends across a sample of large U.S. cities, indicates that the first half of 2026 continued the broad downward trajectory in crime observed in prior years. Of the thirteen offense categories tracked, nine recorded declines compared with the same period in 2025. Against this general backdrop of falling crime, however, reported domestic violence incidents rose by 8 percent.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-22 |title=Crime Trends in U.S. Cities: Mid-Year 2026 Update - Council on Criminal Justice |url=https://counciloncj.org/crime-trends-in-u-s-cities-mid-year-2026-update/ |access-date=2026-09-07 |website=counciloncj.org |language=en-GB}}</ref>

====During pregnancy====
{{Main|Domestic violence and pregnancy}}
The United States was one of the countries identified by a United Nations study with a high rate of domestic violence resulting in death during pregnancy {{citation needed|date=October 2024}}.

====During one's lifetime====
* According to The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and The National Institute of Justice, nearly 25% of women experience at least one physical assault during adulthood by a partner.<ref name=VAWA2005/>
* 22% of the women had been subject to domestic violence during some period of their life, according to a [[United Nations]] study. Since this population included women who had never been married or partnered, the prevalence of domestic violence may have been greater.<ref name=UN54/>
* According to a report by the [[United States Department of Justice]] in 2000, a survey of 16,000 Americans showed 22.1 percent of women and 7.4 percent of men reported being physically assaulted by a current or former spouse, cohabiting partner, boyfriend or girlfriend, or date in their lifetime.<ref name=Tjaden>{{cite web|url=http://www.ncjrs.gov/txtfiles1/nij/183781.txt|title=Full Report of the Prevalence, Incidence, and Consequences of Violence Against Women|publisher=National Institute of Justice, United States Department of Justice|first1=Patricia|last1=Tjaden|first2=Nancy|last2=Thoennes|date=November 2000|access-date=2011-11-18|archive-date=2010-08-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100808022611/http://www.ncjrs.gov/txtfiles1/nij/183781.txt|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 60% of American Indian and Alaska Native women will be physically assaulted in their lifetime.<ref name=VAWA2005/>
* A 2013 report by the American [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) found that 26% of male homosexuals and 44% of lesbians surveyed reported experiencing intimate partner violence. The study evaluated 2010 data from the National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey, which involved over 16,000 U.S. adults.<ref name=lgbt>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-gays-violence-idUSBRE90O11W20130125|first=Susan|last=Heavey|title=Data shows domestic violence, rape an issue for gays|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=October 31, 2013|date=January 25, 2013|archive-date=April 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403023200/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-gays-violence-idUSBRE90O11W20130125|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Injury====
In 1992, domestic violence was the leading cause of injury for women between 15 and 44; more than rapes, muggings, and car accidents combined.<ref>"Violence Against Women, A Majority Staff Report," Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, 102nd Congress, October 1992, p.3.</ref> The levels of domestic injury against men have not been investigated to the same extent.

====Rape====
{{main|Rape}}
* 1 in 71 men and 1 in 5 women have experienced an attempted or completed rape (with 1 in 21 men being made to penetrate someone). More than one in three American Indian and Alaska Native women will be raped in their lifetimes.<ref name=VAWA2005/><ref>"Prevalence, Incidence, and Consequences of Violence Against Women." U.S. Department of Justice. November 1998. Retrieved November 20, 2011.</ref>
* A 2013 CDC study stated that 28% of straight women who had been raped experienced their first rape as a child, with the crime taking place between the ages of 11 and 17.<ref name=lgbt/>

====Murder====
[[File:United States family homicides by relationship 1980 2008.svg|right|thumb|Comparative rates of homicides involving family members between 1980 and 2008. Killing by a spouse or ex-spouse exceeds the rate of all other categories. In proportion to the total number of family homicides, killing by spouses and ex-spouses fell from 52% to 37% during this period. Meanwhile, murder of the children went up 57%.<ref name="htus">{{cite report
 |last1        = Cooper
 |first1       = Alexia D.
 |last2        = Smith
 |first2       = Erica L.
 |date         = 2011-11-16
 |title        = Homicide Trends in the United States, 1980-2008
 |url          = https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/htus8008.pdf
 |publisher    = [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]]
 |pages        = 21
 |id           = NCJ 236018
 |access-date  = 2018-05-14
 |archive-date = 2018-05-03
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20180503100736/https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/htus8008.pdf
 |url-status   = live
}}</ref>]]
Women are more likely than men to be murdered by an intimate partner. Of those killed by an intimate partner, about three quarters are female and about a quarter are male. In 1999 in the United States, 1,218 women and 424 men were killed by an intimate partner,<ref name="usdoj1993">[http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/pub/pdf/ipv01.pdf Intimate Partner Violence, 1993-2001] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090726151815/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov//bjs///pub/pdf/ipv01.pdf |date=2009-07-26 }}</ref> and 1,181 females and 329 males were killed by their intimate partners in 2005.<ref name="cdc.gov">{{Cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/violencePrevention/intimatepartnerviolence/consequences.html |title=CDC - Injury - Intimate Partner Violence Consequences |publisher=Cdc.gov |date=2009-12-14 |access-date=2010-04-26 |archive-date=2010-01-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100129161946/http://www.cdc.gov/violencePrevention/intimatepartnerviolence/consequences.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="theduluthmodel.org">{{Cite web|url=http://www.theduluthmodel.org/wheelgallery.php |title=Domestic Abuse Intervention Programs, Home of the Duluth Model |publisher=Theduluthmodel.org |access-date=2010-04-26 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728093413/http://www.theduluthmodel.org/wheelgallery.php |archive-date=2011-07-28 }}</ref>
In 2007, 2,340 deaths were caused by intimate partner violence—making up 14% of all homicides. 70% of these deaths were females and 30% were males.<ref>{{cite web|title=Understanding Intimate Partner Violence|url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/ipv-factsheet.pdf|publisher=cdc.gov|access-date=24 November 2014|archive-date=10 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510022246/https://www.cdc.gov/ViolencePrevention/pdf/IPV-FactSheet.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

In the United States, firearms have played a role in domestic violence. Compared to other nations, the United States is the number one country for owning guns in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lynch |first1=Kellie R. |last2=Logan |first2=Tk |last3=Jackson |first3=Dylan B. |date=June 2018 |title="People Will Bury Their Guns before They Surrender Them": Implementing Domestic Violence Gun Control in Rural, Appalachian versus Urban Communities |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ruso.12206 |journal=Rural Sociology |volume=83 |issue=2 |pages=315–346 |doi=10.1111/ruso.12206 |issn=0036-0112 |via=Wiley|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to the [[National Coalition Against Domestic Violence]] (NCADV), there has been a rise of 500% of death when a firearm is present during domestic violence.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NCADV {{!}} National Coalition Against Domestic Violence |url=https://ncadv.org/STATISTICS |access-date=2024-03-31 |website=ncadv.org }}</ref>

====Dating violence====
{{main|Dating abuse|Teen dating violence}}
Dating violence is often a precursor to domestic violence. 22% of high school girls and 32% of college women experienced dating violence in a 2000 study. 20.6% of women experienced two or more types of dating violence and 8.3% of women experienced rape, stalking or physical aggression while dating.<ref name=UN42>[https://www.un.org/ga/search/view_doc.asp?symbol=A/61/122/Add.1 ''In-depth study on all forms of violence against women.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131129135804/http://www.un.org/ga/search/view_doc.asp?symbol=A%2F61%2F122%2FAdd.1 |date=2013-11-29 }} United Nations, General Assembly. 6 July 2006. Page 42. Retrieved 16 November 2011.</ref> The levels of dating violence against men has not been investigated to the same extent.

====Stalking====
According to the [[Centers for Disease Control]] National Intimate Partner Violence Survey results of 2010, 1 in 6 women (15.2%) have been stalked during their lifetime, compared to 1 in 19 men (5.7%).<ref>{{cite web|title=National Data on Intimate Partner Violence, Sexual Violence, and Stalking|url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/nisvs-fact-sheet-2014.pdf|publisher=cdc.gov|access-date=24 November 2014|archive-date=8 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141208030823/http://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/nisvs-fact-sheet-2014.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>
Additionally, 1 in 3 bisexual women (37%) and 1 in 6 heterosexual women (16%) have experienced stalking victimization in their lifetime during which they felt very fearful or believed that they or someone close to them would be harmed or killed.<ref>{{cite web|title=NISVS: An Overview of 2010 Findings on Victimization by Sexual Orientation|url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/cdc_nisvs_victimization_final-a.pdf|website=Center for Disease Control|publisher=cdc.gov|access-date=2017-09-09|archive-date=2014-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141028012540/http://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/cdc_nisvs_victimization_final-a.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Socio-economic impacts==
While domestic violence crosses all [[Social class in the United States|socio-economic classes]], Intimate Terrorism (IT) is more prevalent among poor people. When evaluating situational couple violence, poor people, subject to greater strains, have the highest percentage of situational couple violence, which does not necessarily involve serious violence.<ref name=CLASP3 />{{rp|4}}

Regarding ethnicity, socio-economic standing and other factors often have more to do with rates of domestic violence. When comparing the African American population to European Americans by socio-economic class, the rates of domestic violence are roughly the same. Since there are more poor African Americans, though, there is a higher incidence of domestic violence overall. It is not possible to evaluate the rate of domestic violence by ethnicity alone, because of the variability of cultural, economic and historical influences and the forms of domestic violence (situational couple violence, intimate terrorism) affecting each population of people.<ref name=CLASP3 />{{rp|4}}

== Mental Health impacts ==
Domestic Violence is closely linked to mental health outcomes. In research done by Mazza et al. (2021),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mazza |first1=Marianna |last2=Marano |first2=Giuseppe |last3=del Castillo |first3=Angela Gonsalez |last4=Chieffo |first4=Daniela |last5=Monti |first5=Laura |last6=Janiri |first6=Delfina |last7=Moccia |first7=Lorenzo |last8=Sani |first8=Gabriele |date=2021-06-19 |title=Intimate partner violence: A loop of abuse, depression and victimization |journal=World Journal of Psychiatry |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=215–221 |doi=10.5498/wjp.v11.i6.215 |doi-access=free |issn=2220-3206|pmc=8209536 }}</ref> domestic violence was described as a recurring cycle that often leads to an increase in depression and other mental health disorders. This, in turn, tends to heighten the victim's vulnerability to further abuse. This study emphasizes the importance of addressing the psychological dimensions of abuse through comprehensive treatment as well as support services.

Similarly, a study called Deconstructing Stigma: Domestic Violence, Trauma, and Mental Health Support (2025),<ref>{{Citation |title=Domestic Violence, Trauma, and Mental Health |date=2008 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Interpersonal Violence |url=https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412963923.n129 |access-date=2025-11-11 |place=2455 Teller Road, Thousand Oaks California 91320 United States |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc. |doi=10.4135/9781412963923.n129 |isbn=978-1-4129-1800-8|url-access=subscription }}</ref> found that 20% percent of survivors will develop a mental health condition following abuse, including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance abuse disorders. These studies highlight the importance of having trauma-informed care and sensitive interventions to break the cycle of abuse.

===Effects on children===
Up to 10 to 20% children in the United States witness abuse of a parent or caregiver annually. As a result, they are more likely to experience neglect or abuse, less likely to succeed at school, have poor problem-solving skills, subject to higher incidence of emotional and behavioral problems, and more likely to tolerate violence in their adult relationships.<ref>Child Welfare Information Gateway (2009). [http://www.childwelfare.gov/pubs/factsheets/domesticviolence.cfm ''Domestic Violence and the Child Welfare System.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111129130945/http://www.childwelfare.gov/pubs/factsheets/domesticviolence.cfm |date=2011-11-29 }} Administration for Children & Families, U.S. Department of Health & Human Services. Retrieved December 9, 2011.</ref> In the wake of domestic violence, parental psychopathology can further compromise the quality of parenting, and in turn, increase the risk for the child's developing emotional and behavioral difficulties if mental health care is not sought.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Schechter | first1 = DS | last2 = Willheim | first2 = E | last3 = McCaw | first3 = J | last4 = Turner | first4 = JB | last5 = Myers | first5 = MM | last6 = Zeanah | first6 = CH | year = 2011 | title = The relationship of violent fathers, posttraumatically stressed mothers, and symptomatic children in a preschool-age inner-city pediatrics clinic sample | journal = Journal of Interpersonal Violence | volume = 26 | issue = 18| pages = 3699–3719 | doi=10.1177/0886260511403747 | pmid=22170456| s2cid = 206562093 }}</ref>

In a study done by Bhuller et al. (2024),<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://doi.org/10.3386/w30792 |title=Domestic Violence and the Mental Health and Well-being of Victims and Their Children |last1=Bhuller |first1=Manudeep |last2=Dahl |first2=Gordon |last3=Løken |first3=Katrine |last4=Mogstad |first4=Magne |date=December 2022 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |doi=10.3386/w30792 |location=Cambridge, MA|hdl=11250/3037651 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> it was found that children of domestic violence victims experience increased mental health visits, around 19% higher than children who are unexposed to this type of violence. Domestic violence also contributes to higher divorce rates, which have long lasting impacts on the children and families of the victims.

===Homelessness===
{{Main|Homeless women in the United States}}

According to the authors of "Housing Problems and Domestic Violence," 38% of domestic violence victims will become homeless in their lifetime.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acf.hhs.gov/fysb/resource/dv-homelessness-stats-2016|title=Domestic Violence and Homelessness: Statistics (2016)|website=Family & Youth Services Bureau|access-date=2018-01-15|archive-date=2018-01-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180116081214/https://www.acf.hhs.gov/fysb/resource/dv-homelessness-stats-2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=VAWA2005/> Domestic violence is the direct cause of homelessness for over half of all homeless women in the United States.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2105/AJPH.88.9.1325 |vauthors=Ringwalt CL, Greene JM, Robertson M, McPheeters M |title=The prevalence of homelessness among adolescents in the United States |journal=Am J Public Health |volume=88 |issue=9 |pages=1325–9 |date=September 1998 |pmid=9736871 |pmc=1509094 }}</ref>
According to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, domestic violence is the third leading cause of homelessness among families.<ref>{{cite web|title=Domestic Violence: Statistics & Facts|url=http://www.safehorizon.org/page/domestic-violence-statistics--facts-52.html|website=Safe Horizon|access-date=24 November 2014|archive-date=24 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141124081525/http://www.safehorizon.org/page/domestic-violence-statistics--facts-52.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Economic impacts===
Economic abuse can occur across all socio-economic levels.<ref>{{cite web|title=Economic Abuse |url=http://www.ncadv.org/files/EconomicAbuse.pdf |website=National Coalition Against Domestic Violence |publisher=The Public Policy Office of the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence |access-date=24 November 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130228065620/http://www.ncadv.org/files/EconomicAbuse.pdf |archive-date=28 February 2013 }}</ref>

The [[National Coalition Against Domestic Violence]] in the [[United States]] reports that:
* 25% - 50% of victims of abuse from a partner have lost their job due to domestic violence.
* 35% - 56% of victims of domestic violence are harassed at work by their partners.
* More than 1.75 million workdays are lost each year to domestic violence. Lost productivity due to missed workdays and decreased productivity, with increased health and safety costs, results in a loss of $3 to $5 billion each year.<ref name=ncadv>[http://www.ncadv.org/files/EconomicAbuse.pdf ''Economic Abuse.''] {{webarchive |url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20150110104816/http://www.ncadv.org/files/EconomicAbuse.pdf |date=January 10, 2015 }} National Coalition Against Domestic Violence. Retrieved November 20, 2011.</ref>

The [[Centers for Disease Control]] has released that the medical care, mental health services, and lost productivity cost of intimate partner violence was an estimated $8.3 billion in 2003 dollars for women alone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Understanding Intimate Partner Violence|url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/ipv-factsheet.pdf|website=Centers for Disease Control|publisher=cdc.gov|access-date=2017-09-09|archive-date=2019-05-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510022246/https://www.cdc.gov/ViolencePrevention/pdf/IPV-FactSheet.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Religion==
{{main|Christianity and domestic violence|Islam and domestic violence}}

One 2004 study by [[William Bradford Wilcox]] examined the relationship between religious affiliation, church attendance, and domestic violence, using data on wives' reports of spousal violence from three national [[United States]] surveys conducted between 1992 and 1994.<ref name=wilcox>Wilcox, William Bradford. ''Soft Patriarchs, New Men: How Christianity Shapes Fathers and Husbands''. [[University of Chicago Press]] (2004), [https://books.google.com/books?id=s0cY1rWfxKUC&pg=PA181 p181-82]. {{ISBN|0-226-89709-5}}.</ref> The study found that the lowest reported rates of domestic violence occurred among active conservative Protestants (2.8% of husbands committed domestic violence), followed by those who were religiously unaffiliated (3.2%), nominal mainline Protestants (3.9%), active mainline Protestants (5.4%), and nominal conservative Protestants (7.2%).<ref name=wilcox/>

Overall (including both nominal and active members), the rates among conservative Protestants and mainline Protestants were 4.8% and 4.3%, respectively.<ref name=wilcox/> Examining Wilcox's study, Van Leewen finds that the parenting style of conservative Protestant fathers is characterized by features which have been linked to positive outcomes among children and adolescents,{{#tag:ref|"He concludes that conservative Protestant fathers' neotraditional parenting style seems to be closer to the authoritative style—characterized by moderately high levels of parental control and high levels of parental supportiveness—that has been linked to positive outcomes among children and adolescents."|group=nb}}<ref name=VanLeeuwen>Van Leeuwen, 'Social Sciences', in Husbands & Larsen, 'Women, ministry and the Gospel: Exploring new paradigms', p. 194 (2007).</ref> that there is no evidence that gender-traditionalist ideology of the "soft patriarchal" kind is a strong predictor of domestic physical abuse,{{#tag:ref|'The upshot is that we have no evidence so far that a gender-traditionalist ideology—at least of the soft patriarchal variety—is a strong predictor of domestic physical abuse.'|group=nb}}<ref name=VanLeeuwen/> and that "gender hierarchicalist males" who are frequent and active church members function positively in the domestic environment. {{#tag:ref|"Gender hierarchicalist males—at least those who have frequent and active church involvement—turn out, on average, to be better men than their theories: more often than not, they are functional egalitarians, and the rhetoric of male headship may actually be functioning as a covert plea for greater male responsibility and nurturant involvement on the home front."|group=nb}}<ref name=VanLeeuwen/>

Another 2007 study by [[Christopher Ellison (sociologist)|Christopher G. Ellison]] suggested that "religious involvement, specifically church attendance, protects against domestic violence, and this protective effect is stronger for African American men and women and for Hispanic men, groups that, for a variety of reasons, experience elevated risk for this type of violence."<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ellison | first1 = Christopher G. | year = 2007 | title = Race/Ethnicity, Religious Involvement, and Domestic Violence | journal = Violence Against Women | volume = 13 | issue = 11| pages = 1094–1112 | doi=10.1177/1077801207308259| pmid = 17951587 | s2cid = 44721781 | doi-access = }}</ref>

==History==
Prior to the mid-1800s, most legal systems implicitly accepted wife beating as a valid exercise of a husband's authority over his wife.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Domestic violence|encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica Online|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/168589/domestic-violence|access-date=October 31, 2011|quote=In the early 1800s most legal systems implicitly accepted wife-beating as a husband's right, part of his entitlement to control over the resources and services of his wife.|archive-date=November 23, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111123075833/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/168589/domestic-violence|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Daniels1997>{{cite book|last=Daniels|first=Cynthia R.|title=Feminists Negotiate the State: The Politics of Domestic Violence|year=1997|publisher=Univ. Press of America|location=Lanham|isbn=978-0-7618-0884-8|pages=5–10}}</ref> One exception, however, was the 1641 [[Massachusetts Body of Liberties|Body of Liberties of the Massachusetts Bay colonists]], which declared that a married woman should be "free from bodilie correction or stripes by her husband."<ref>[http://history.hanover.edu/texts/masslib.htm The Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111115195305/http://history.hanover.edu/texts/masslib.htm |date=2011-11-15 }} at Hanover Historical Texts Project.</ref>

Political agitation during the 19th century led to changes in both popular opinion and legislation regarding domestic violence within the [[United Kingdom]] and the [[United States]].<ref name=Britannica>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Domestic violence|encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica Online|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/168589/domestic-violence|access-date=October 31, 2011|quote=Feminist agitation in the 1800s produced a sea change in public opinion...|archive-date=November 23, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111123075833/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/168589/domestic-violence|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Gordon2002>{{cite book|last=Gordon|first=Linda|title=Heroes of Their Own Lives: The Politics and History of Family Violence|year=2002|publisher=University of Illinois Press|location=Urbana|isbn=978-0-252-07079-2|pages=253–255}}</ref> In 1850, Tennessee became the first state in the United States to explicitly outlaw wife beating.<ref>{{cite book|last=Kleinberg|first=S. J.|title=Women in the United States, 1830-1945|year=1999|publisher=Rutgers University Press|isbn=978-0-8135-2729-1|page=[https://archive.org/details/womeninunitedsta0000klei/page/143 143]|url=https://archive.org/details/womeninunitedsta0000klei/page/143}}</ref><ref name=Pleck1989>{{cite journal|last=Pleck|first=Elizabeth|title=Criminal Approaches to Family Violence|journal=Family Violence|year=1989|volume=11}}</ref> Other states soon followed suit.<ref name=Daniels1997/><ref name=Pleck1979>{{cite journal|last=Pleck|first=Elizabeth|title=Wife Beating in Nineteenth-Century America|journal=Victimology|year=1979|volume=4|pages=64–65}}</ref>

In 1878, the [[Matrimonial Causes Act]] made it possible for women in the UK to seek separations from abusive husbands.<ref name=Arnot2003>{{cite book|last=Arnot|first=Margaret L.|title=Gender and crime in modern Europe|year=2003|publisher=Routledge|location=London|isbn=978-1-85728-746-2|edition=[Online-Ausg.]|author2=Usborne, Cornelie|page=123}}</ref> By the end of the 1870s, most courts in the United States were uniformly opposed to the right of husbands to physically discipline their wives.<ref>Green, Nicholas St. John. 1879. ''Criminal Law Reports: Being Reports of Cases Determined in the Federal and State Courts of the United States, and in the Courts of England, Ireland, Canada, etc. with notes''. Hurd and Houghton. "The cases in the American courts are uniform against the right of the husband to use any [physical] chastisement, moderate or otherwise, toward the wife, for any purpose."</ref> By the early 20th century, it was common for the police to intervene in cases of domestic violence in the United States, but arrests remained rare.<ref name=Feder1999>{{cite book|last=Feder|first=Lynette|title=Women and Domestic Violence: An Interdisciplinary Approach|year=1999|publisher=Haworth Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-7890-0667-7|page=22}}</ref> Wife beating was made illegal in all states of the United States by 1920.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/No-drop%20prosecution%20of%20domestic%20violence:%20just%20good%20policy,%20or%20equal...-a058511048|title=No-drop prosecution of domestic violence: just good policy, or equal protection mandate? - Free Online Library|website=Thefreelibrary.com|access-date=16 December 2016|archive-date=1 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101135451/https://www.thefreelibrary.com/No-drop%20prosecution%20of%20domestic%20violence:%20just%20good%20policy,%20or%20equal...-a058511048|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/topic/Domestic_violence.aspx|title=Domestic violence facts, information, pictures - Encyclopedia.com articles about Domestic violence|website=Encyclopedia.com|access-date=16 December 2016|archive-date=3 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160903153253/http://www.encyclopedia.com/topic/Domestic_violence.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

Modern attention to domestic violence began in the [[women's movement]] of the 1970s, particularly within [[feminism]] and [[women's rights]], as concern about wives being beaten by their husbands gained attention. The first known use of the expression "domestic violence" in a modern context, meaning "spouse abuse, violence in the home" was in 1973.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.womensaid.org.uk/landing_page.asp?section=00010001001900040004 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061006133850/http://www.womensaid.org.uk/landing_page.asp?section=00010001001900040004 | url-status=dead | archive-date=2006-10-06 | title=Our history - 1970s}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1973/jul/16/battered-wives|title=BATTERED WIVES (Hansard, 16 July 1973)|website=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-date=24 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024231056/http://hansard.millbanksystems.com/commons/1973/jul/16/battered-wives|date=16 July 1973|url-status=live}}</ref> With the rise of the [[men's movement]] of the 1990s, the problem of [[domestic violence against men]] has also gained significant attention.

The Thurman lawsuit (''[[Thurman v. City of Torrington]]'', DC, 595 F.Supp. 1521 (1985)) brought about sweeping national reform of domestic violence laws, including the "Thurman Law" (aka the Family Violence Prevention and Response Act) instituted in Connecticut in 1986, making domestic violence an automatically arrestable offense, even if the victim does not wish to press charges.<ref name="auto1">{{cite web |url=http://cyber.law.harvard.edu/vaw00/thurmanexcerpt.html |title=Thurman v. City of Torrington |publisher=harvard.edu |access-date=2011-09-04 |archive-date=2016-08-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809225822/http://cyber.law.harvard.edu/vaw00/thurmanexcerpt.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Attention to violence against men began in the late 1980s.

Congress designated October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month in 1989.<ref>Letts, Sharon. "[http://infoweb.newsbank.com/iw-search/we/InfoWeb?p_product=AWNB&p_theme=aggregated5&p_action=doc&p_docid=123786EC186139E8&p_docnum=288&p_queryname=8 Nesting: Making a loving nest]". ''Times-Standard'' (Eureka, California). September 25, 2008.</ref> Such legislation has passed every year since with the [[National Coalition Against Domestic Violence]] providing key leadership.<ref name=":Month2">"[https://nrcdv.org/dvam/DVAM-history History] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612140138/https://nrcdv.org/dvam/DVAM-history |date=2018-06-12 }}". ''Domestic Violence Awareness Project''. Retrieved June 8, 2018.</ref><ref name="dvam">Thompson, Bill. "[http://infoweb.newsbank.com/iw-search/we/InfoWeb?p_product=AWNB&p_theme=aggregated5&p_action=doc&p_docid=0EB0F72E8990EFAA&p_docnum=3&p_queryname=4 Awareness of domestic violence increases in October]". ''The Tampa Tribune''. October 1, 1997.</ref><ref>Magrath, Shawn. "[http://infoweb.newsbank.com/iw-search/we/InfoWeb?p_product=AWNB&p_theme=aggregated5&p_action=doc&p_docid=158CE05E5C2EEB88&p_docnum=11&p_queryname=9 Catholic Charities recognizes Domestic Violence Awareness Month]". ''The Evening Sun'' (Norwich, New York). October 29, 2015.</ref>

Recent legal scholarship argues that the traditional narrative surrounding domestic violence, that judges ignored or shielded wife beaters behind the veil of marital privacy, is questionable.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Katz |first=Elizabeth D. |date=2015 |title=Judicial Patriarchy and Domestic Violence: A Challenge to the Conventional Family Privacy Narrative |url=https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=2589941 |url-status=live |journal=William & Mary Journal of Women and the Law |location=Rochester, NY |volume=21 |issue=2 |ssrn=2589941 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520171147/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2589941 |archive-date=2022-05-20 |access-date=2021-11-03}}</ref> Rather, judges would routinely intervene on behalf of battered women in order to protect victims and reinforce gender norms by punishing men for "failing to conform to appropriate husbandly behavior."<ref name=":1" /> On the other hand, women accused of beating their husbands were not punished as severely and were even sometimes applauded by judges for "disciplining" their husbands.<ref name=":1" />

== Prevalence ==
Several National studies consistently show that domestic violence remains a widespread issue in the United States. It is estimated that one in four women will experience domestic violence at some point during their lives, which is why it is amongst the most common forms of gender based violence in the United States. Prevalence will vary due to several different circumstantial issues like social isolation, access to healthcare, poverty, and housing instability (Ballard Brief, 2025).<ref name="Gray 2024 1–13">{{Citation |last=Gray |first=Amber Deneén |chapter=Domestic Violence Against Immigrant Women and Children in the United States |date=2024 |title=Encyclopedia of Domestic Violence |pages=1–13 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-85493-5_426-1 |access-date=2025-11-17 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-85493-5}}</ref> All of these contribute to hyper vulnerability, and they affect many marginalized groups. The prevalence of domestic violence can also be shaped by intergenerational patterns, meaning that children who grow up with such violence are more likely to perpetrate that same violence in future intimate relationships (Ballard Brief, 2025).<ref name="Gray 2024 1–13"/>

== The Cycle Of Abuse ==
Abusive Relationships exhibit a pattern known as the cycle of domestic violence. This cycle is why victims have a difficult time leaving their abusers.

* First there is the tension building stage where the victim feels like they have to be cautious around the abuser as to not upset them.<ref name="doi.org">{{Cite journal |title=National Health Resource Center on Domestic Violence |url=https://doi.org/10.1037/e596232012-001 |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=PsycEXTRA Dataset |doi=10.1037/e596232012-001 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Second there is the abusive incident. This is a violent incident that occurs between the abuser and victim including, physical, emotional, or sexual abuse.<ref name="doi.org"/>
* And lastly there is the honeymoon phase where the abuser attempts to make up for what they have done by apologizing, gifting things to the victim, and promising not to hurt them again. These are all attempts to get the victim to stay in the relationship.<ref name="doi.org"/>

== Early Indicators and Dating Violence ==
Adolescent relationship violence is an early indicator of possible future domestic abuse. Matud (2007)<ref>{{Citation |last1=Anderson |first1=A. |title=Social Theory: Dating Violence |date=2025 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Domestic Violence |pages=1–6 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-85493-5_2196-1 |access-date=2025-11-11 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer Nature Switzerland |isbn=978-3-030-85493-5 |last2=Running |first2=S. |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-85493-5_2196-1 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> demonstrates that dating violence in youth often mirrors adult patterns of power imbalance and control issues. Gender norms and the normalization of aggression in youth relationships are also contributing factors to intimate partner violence down the line. Early education and intervention programs are crucial for potentially reducing aggressive behaviors in later adult relationships. Research that has been done in this area further suggests that harmful relationship patterns form during adolescence and can solidify in adult life, which is why early intervention is crucial. Programs that emphasize open communication and conflict resolution skills mitigate some of these risks by addressing the behavior early on. Educators and Policymakers may help prevent the developmental pathways that lead to domestic violence in adult life.

== Public Perception of Intimate Partner Violence ==
In a study conducted by Groggel and Rojas (2023)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Groggel |first1=Anne |last2=Rojas |first2=Fabio |date=January 2023 |title=How Americans Assess Intimate Partner Violence: Evidence from a Survey Experiment |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231221149627 |journal=Socius: Sociological Research for a Dynamic World |volume=9 |article-number=23780231221149627 |doi=10.1177/23780231221149627 |issn=2378-0231|doi-access=free }}</ref> it was found that American public perceptions of intimate partner violence often vary due to contextual factors like the presence of a firearm or the race of the victim and the abuser. The participants in this study were less likely to support restricting gun ownership by abusers in cases where it involved black victims. This study demonstrated how racial bias can influence public concern and perceived severity in cases of domestic violence. The findings of this study suggest that stereotypes often shape how the public views victims and if they are "worthy" of intervention. This study also highlights how radicalized attitudes indirectly affect policy preferences. The biases found in these studies contribute to unequal support for domestic violence victims and contribute to inconsistent accountability for the abusers.

==Law==
Victims of domestic violence are offered legal remedies that are both civil and criminal in nature.
* Criminal law remedies include the criminal prosecution of the offender, and possible restraints on the offender's behavior during periods of pretrial release or as part of a criminal sentence.
* Civil law remedies include the possibility of obtaining a [[protection order]].
These remedies are not exclusive, meaning that a victim may seek both the criminal prosecution of the offender and also petition for civil remedies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fagan |first=Jeffrey |date=January 1996 |title=The Criminalization of Domestic Violence: Promises and Limits |url=https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles/crimdom.pdf |journal=National Institute of Justice Research Report |pages=1–65 |via=US Department of Justice}}</ref>

People who perpetrate acts of domestic violence are subject to criminal prosecution. Prosecution most often occurs under [[assault]] and [[Battery (crime)|battery]] laws. Perpetrators of domestic violence can be charged under general statutes,<ref name="childwelfare1">{{cite web |url=https://www.childwelfare.gov/systemwide/laws_policies/statutes/defdomvio.cfm |title=Definitions of Domestic Violence |publisher=Childwelfare.gov |access-date=2013-09-08 |archive-date=2014-12-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141215012201/https://www.childwelfare.gov/systemwide/laws_policies/statutes/defdomvio.cfm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t16c025.php |title=South Carolina Legislature Mobile |publisher=Scstatehouse.gov |access-date=2013-09-08 |archive-date=2013-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130821093259/http://scstatehouse.gov/code/t16c025.php |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.courtinnovation.org/sites/default/files/Case_Processing_Report.pdf|title=A Comparison of Two Prosecution Policies in Cases of Intimate Partner Violence Mandatory Case Filing vs. Following the Victim's Lead|website=Courtinnovation.org|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-date=13 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180213031523/https://www.courtinnovation.org/sites/default/files/Case_Processing_Report.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> but most states have also enacted specific statutes that specifically criminalize acts of domestic violence. For example, under the South Carolina code, the crime of "Criminal domestic violence" states that "''it is unlawful to: (1) cause physical harm or injury to a person's own household member; or (2) offer or attempt to cause physical harm or injury to a person's own household member with apparent present ability under circumstances reasonably creating fear of imminent peril''." If aggravated circumstances are present, people can be charged with the crime of "Criminal domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature."

Other possible criminal charges may be brought based upon the facts of the offense, potentially including charges such as [[harassment]], [[menacing]] or [[false imprisonment]].

Acts of domestic violence can have a significant impact on [[child custody|Child custody laws in the United States]] litigation, most notably when an act of domestic violence is committed in the presence of the minor child. A parent with a history of domestic violence may be at a significant disadvantage in a custody case, even if the domestic violence was not directed at the other parent.

Certain laws indirectly impact domestic abuse survivors. A study commissioned by the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] of two cities in New York found that local nuisance ordinances, which penalize tenants and property owners based on criminal or police activity on a property, may have the unintended consequence of victims of domestic abuse being evicted and/or deterred from reporting abuse.<ref>[https://www.aclu.org/report/silenced-how-nuisance-ordinances-punish-crime-victims-new-york Silenced: How Nuisance Ordinances Punish Crime Victims in New York] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180227060640/https://www.aclu.org/report/silenced-how-nuisance-ordinances-punish-crime-victims-new-york |date=2018-02-27 }}. June 2015. Social Science Research Council.</ref> In a study of four cities in [[Cuyahoga County, Ohio]] found survivors of domestic violence were disproportionately likely to receive a nuisance notification.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mead |first1=Joseph |last2=Hatch |first2=Megan E. |last3=Tighe |first3=J. Rosie |last4=Pappas |first4=Marissa |last5=Andrasik |first5=Kristi |last6=Bonham |first6=Elizabeth |title=Treating neighbors as nuisances: Troubling applications of criminal activity nuisance ordinances |journal=Cleveland State Law Review et Cetera |date=2018 |volume=66 |pages=1–15 |url=http://www.clevstlrev.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/66-Clev-St-L-Rev-Et-Cetera-3-2018-Treating-Neighbors-As-Nuisances-by-Joseph-Mead-et-al.pdf |access-date=2019-03-11 |archive-date=2020-07-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200725071222/http://www.clevstlrev.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/66-Clev-St-L-Rev-Et-Cetera-3-2018-Treating-Neighbors-As-Nuisances-by-Joseph-Mead-et-al.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

The lockdowns that were part of the [[U.S. state and local government response to the 2020 coronavirus pandemic|2020 coronavirus response]] may have indirectly contributed to an increase in domestic violence. Domestic violence calls to police within New York state, for example, increased by 15–20% in March 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/coronavirus-covid-19-domestic-violence-surge_n_5e8b137fc5b6e7d76c672a4c|title=UN Chief Condemns 'Horrifying Global Surge' In Domestic Violence|last=Fang|first=Marina|date=2020-04-06|website=HuffPost|access-date=2020-04-06|archive-date=2020-04-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200407005152/https://www.huffpost.com/entry/coronavirus-covid-19-domestic-violence-surge_n_5e8b137fc5b6e7d76c672a4c|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Violence Against Women Acts===
[[File:United_States_Military,_Domestic_Violence_Awareness_Month_Poster_September_2011.jpg|thumb|October is observed as Domestic Violence Awareness Month (DVAM) in the United States. This poster was issued by various branches of the United States military to educate and prevent domestic abuse.]]
{{main|Violence Against Women Act}}

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) was originally passed in 1994, and reauthorized in 2005, 2013, and 2022. These federal laws work to end domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking through the creation of new programs and legislation within the Department of Justice and Health and Human Services. Along with the passage of provisions to legislation, the [[Office on Violence Against Women]] came to fruition in 1995 under the Department of Justice of the United States to continue efforts that would protect women. The primary role of the division was to evaluate and improve outcomes for domestic violence survivors through tackling related issues like housing insecurity.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Sacco |first=Lisa |date=May 26, 2015 |title=The Violence Against Women Act: Overview, Legislation, and Federal Funding |url=https://www.utsystem.edu/sites/default/files/offices/police/files/annual-promotional-exams/vawa.pdf}}</ref> One of the contributions of the OVAW was the introduction of federal grants to incentivize agencies to help women in need.<ref name=":02" /> The VAWA intensified investigations and prosecutions of individuals involved in domestic abuse cases and it decreased the number of occurrences. The law helped victim advocates and government agencies work together, created prevention and victim support programs, and resulted in new punishments for certain violent crimes, which by 2005 resulted in:

* 49.8% reduction of non-fatal, violent victimizations committed by intimate partners.
* In the first six years, an estimated $14.8 billion in net averted social costs.
* 51% increase in reporting of domestic violence and 18% increase in National Domestic Violence Hotline calls each year, evidence that as victims become aware of remedies, they break the code of silence.<ref name="VAWA2005" /><ref name="US-DHHS">[http://www.womenshealth.gov/violence-against-women/laws-on-violence-against-women/ ''Laws on violence against women.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170628203253/https://www.womenshealth.gov/violence-against-women/laws-on-violence-against-women/|date=2017-06-28}} Office on Women's Health, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. May 18, 2011. Retrieved November 20, 2011.</ref>

''[[United States v. Morrison]]'', 529 U.S. 598 (2000), is a [[U.S. Supreme Court]] decision that held that parts of the [[Violence Against Women Act of 1994]] were unconstitutional because they exceeded the powers granted to the [[US Congress]] under the [[Commerce Clause]] and the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment]]'s [[Equal Protection Clause]]. Along with ''[[United States v. Lopez]]'' (1995), it was part of a series of [[Rehnquist Court]] cases that limited Congress's powers under the Commerce Clause. The Court's 5–4 decision in ''[[United States v. Morrison]]'' invalidated the section of the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 that gave victims of gender-motivated violence the right to sue their attackers in federal court. Chief Justice [[William Rehnquist|Rehnquist]], writing for the majority, held that Congress lacked authority, under either the [[Commerce Clause]] or the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment]], to enact that provision. However, the Act's program funding remained unaffected.

In 2013 additional facets were added to VAWA: new provisions for grant funding; allowing authorization to Native American Tribes to enforce domestic violence laws; and amendments to the [[Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000]].<ref name=":02" />

In 2022 VAWA funding was reauthorized to include the Ensuring Forensic Health Care for all Act (EFCA) to fund support for generalist forensic nurse training.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Holbrook |first=Debra |date=2023-12-20 |title=Violence Against Women Act: Re-authorization and Impact for Forensic Health Professionals |url=https://mrujs.mtroyal.ca/index.php/jafn/article/view/736 |journal=Journal of the Academy of Forensic Nursing |language=en |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=64–68 |doi=10.29173/jafn736 |issn=2817-3848|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Also in 2022, VAWA was amended to include Native Hawaiian survivors of gender-based violence and Native Hawaiian organizations in grant funding.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.civilbeat.org/2022/12/native-hawaiian-domestic-violence-survivors-now-eligible-for-federal-funding/|title=Native Hawaiian Domestic Violence Survivors Now Eligible For Federal Funding|first=Alicia|last=Lou|date=December 31, 2022|website=Honolulu Civil Beat}}</ref>

In the 2024 U.S. Supreme Court case ''[[United States v. Rahimi]]'', the U.S. Supreme Court, in an 8-1 ruling, upheld VAWA’s domestic violence restraining order which restricts firearm possession for people convicted of domestic abuse.<ref name="1968and1994">{{cite news|url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/06/supreme-court-upholds-law-disarming-domestic-abusers/|title=Supreme Court Upholds Law Disarming Domestic Abusers|first=Nina|last=Martin|publisher=Mother Jones|date=June 21, 2024|accessdate=June 21, 2024}}</ref>

===Family Violence Prevention and Services Act===
{{main|Family Violence Prevention and Services Act}}

The Family Violence Prevention and Services Act (FVPSA), first authorized as part of the Child Abuse Amendments of 1984 (PL 98–457), provides federal funding to help victims of domestic violence and their dependent children by providing shelter and related help, offering violence prevention programs, and improving how service agencies work together in communities.
* Formula Grants. This money helps states, territories, and tribes create and support programs that work to help victims and prevent family violence. The amount of money is determined by a formula based partly on population. The states, territories, and tribes distribute the money to thousands of domestic violence shelters and programs.
* The 24-hour, confidential, toll-free [[National Domestic Violence Hotline]]—available since February 1996—provides support, information, referrals, safety planning, and [[crisis intervention]] in more than 200 languages to hundreds of thousands of domestic violence victims each year.<ref>{{cite web |title=25 Years of The Hotline |date=June 9, 2021 |publisher=The Hotline |url=https://www.thehotline.org/about/25-years-of-the-hotline/}}</ref>
* The Domestic Violence Prevention Enhancement and Leadership Through Alliances (DELTA) Program teaches people ways to prevent violence.<ref name="US-DHHS"/>
