======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Sexual harassment
======================================================================

{{short description|Unwanted sexual attention or advances}}
{{other uses}}
{{Use American English|date=February 2020}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2026}}
[[File:Bullying Sexual.JPG|thumb|Acted depiction of a man making an unwelcome sexual advance on a woman by putting his hand on her thigh]]
{{Sex and the law}}

'''Sexual harassment''' primarily refers to [[harassment]] involving [[sexual abuse|unwanted sexual behavior]], though it may occasionally refer to [[sexism|harassment with a sexist targeting pattern]].<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/24994 |title=Sexual Harassment of Women: Climate, Culture, and Consequences in Academic Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |publisher=National Academies Press |others=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine: Committee on the Impacts of Sexual Harassment in Academia; Committee on Women in Science, Engineering, and Medicine; Policy and Global Affairs |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-309-47087-2 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Paula A. |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=24–27 |doi=10.17226/24994 |pmid=29894119 |bibcode=2018nap..book24994N |editor-last2=Widnall |editor-first2=Sheila E. |editor-last3=Benya |editor-first3=Frazier F.}}</ref><ref name=":21" /> Although some types of sexual harassment seem to be motivated by [[sexual desire]], they are more often committed to [[Misogyny|hurt women]] or punish people for violating [[Gender role|gender norms]].<ref name=":22" /> Popular understanding of sexual harassment primarily focuses on sexual coercion and unwanted sexual advances, which are less common than other types of harassment. All types of sexual harassment can harm a victim's physical and mental health and affect their personal and professional lives.<ref name=":7" />

Sexual harassment may involve harassers or victims of any [[gender]], occur between friends or [[catcalling|strangers]], involve equal or [[subordinate]] relationships, and consist of verbal, physical, or indirect actions.<ref name="eeoc">{{cite web | url = http://www.eeoc.gov/laws/types/sexual_harassment.cfm | title = Sexual Harassment | publisher = U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission | access-date = 16 July 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190513132253/https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/types/sexual_harassment.cfm | archive-date = 13 May 2019 | url-status = live }}</ref> Examples may involve insulting sexual or sexist remarks, offensive [[sexual innuendo]], [[indecent exposure]], [[sexting]], [[sexual roleplay]], collecting or disseminating photos of the victim in private moments, demanding or requesting [[sexual favors]] as [[bribery]], and [[sexual assault]] like [[groping]] or [[rape]].<ref name=":21">{{cite book |last1=Paludi |first1=Michele A. |url=https://archive.org/details/academicworkplac0000palu/page/2 |title=Academic and workplace sexual harassment: a resource manual |last2=Barickman |first2=Richard B. |publisher=SUNY Press |year=1991 |isbn=978-0-7914-0830-8 |location=Albany, NY |pages=[https://archive.org/details/academicworkplac0000palu/page/2 2–8] |chapter=Definitions and incidence of academic and workplace sexual harassment |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vx4qhVPOYUUC&pg=PA2}}</ref><ref name="auto">Dziech, Billie Wright; Weiner, Linda. ''The Lecherous Professor: Sexual Harassment on Campus''.{{page needed|date=October 2012}} Chicago Illinois: University of Illinois Press, 1990. {{ISBN|978-0-8070-3100-1}}; Boland, 2002{{page needed|date=October 2012}}</ref>

In most countries, certain types of workplace sexual harassment are illegal as a form of [[employment discrimination]]. The legal and social understanding of sexual harassment varies by culture.<ref name=":15" /> Employment laws do not impose a "general civility code", so they generally do not prohibit minor isolated harassment incidents.<ref>{{caselaw source |case=''Oncale v.Sundowner Offshore Services, Inc.'', 528 U.S. 75 (1998) |findlaw=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-supreme-court/523/75.html |justia=https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/523/75/case.html}}</ref> In many countries, harassment may be considered illegal when it is frequent or severe enough to create a hostile or offensive work environment, or when it results in an adverse employment decision (such as the victim's demotion, firing, or quitting). Over 100 countries have laws against both hostile environment and ''[[quid pro quo]]'' types of sexual harassment, and dozens have laws specifically addressing sexual harassment based on [[sexual orientation]] or [[gender identity]].<ref name=":15" /> For many businesses or organizations, preventing sexual harassment and defending employees from sexual harassment charges have become key goals of legal decision-making.

{{TOC limit|3}}

==Etymology and history==
The term "sexual harassment" was coined in the 1970s, and its meaning and popularity as a concept have grown over time.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Crouch |first=Margaret A. |date=December 1998 |title=The "Social Etymology" of 'Sexual Harassment' |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9833.1998.tb00118.x |journal=Journal of Social Philosophy |language=en |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=19–40 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9833.1998.tb00118.x |issn=0047-2786 |via=Wiley}}</ref> However, the behaviors it describes are common across cultures and eras, and have also been described by other terms. Although discussion of sexual harassment has frequently been silenced and trivialized over time, reports of workplace sexual harassment have been documented since at least the 1600s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Segrave |first=Kerry |title=The Sexual Harassment of Women in the Workplace, 1600 to 1993 |publisher=McFarland |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-7864-7615-2 |edition=Reprint |location=Jefferson, North Carolina |pages=}}</ref>

The framing of sexual harassment as a legal issue also originated in the 1970s.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |title=Catherine &#91;sic&#93; Mackinnon defines sexual harassment as a form of sex discrimination |url=https://www.genderequalitiesat50.ed.ac.uk/timeline/catherine-mackinnon-defines-sexual-harassment-as-a-form-of-sex-discrimination/ |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=The University of Edinburgh – Gender Equalities at Work |language=en-GB}}</ref> Since the 1990s, many countries have adopted laws targeting sexual harassment, and social movements like [[MeToo movement|#MeToo]] have raised awareness of the concept and spurred social and legal change.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Heymann |first1=Jody |last2=Moreno |first2=Gonzalo |last3=Raub |first3=Amy |last4=Sprague |first4=Aleta |date=4 March 2023 |title=Progress Towards Ending Sexual Harassment at Work? A Comparison of Sexual Harassment Policy in 192 Countries |journal=Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis: Research and Practice |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=172–193 |doi=10.1080/13876988.2022.2100698 |issn=1387-6988}}</ref>

=== The term "sexual harassment" ===
<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 June 2024 |title=A Profound Impact |url=https://magazine.swarthmore.edu/issue/spring-summer-2024/a-profound-impact/ |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=Swarthmore College Bulletin |language=en-US}}</ref>

These activists, [[Lin Farley]], Susan Meyer, and Karen Sauvigne, went on to form [[Working Women United]], which, along with the [[Alliance Against Sexual Coercion]] (founded in 1976 by [[Freada Klein]], Lynn Wehrli, and Elizabeth Cohn-Stuntz), was among the pioneer organizations to bring sexual harassment to public attention in the late 1970s.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last=Baker |first=Carrie N. |date=1 October 2007 |title=The Emergence of Organized Feminist Resistance to Sexual Harassment in the United States in the 1970s |url=https://scholarworks.smith.edu/swg_facpubs/12 |journal=Journal of Women's History |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=161–184 |doi=10.1352/jowh.2007.0051 |doi-broken-date=28 January 2026}}</ref> Farley also wrote a book to raise awareness, ''Sexual Shakedown: The Sexual Harassment of Women on the Job'', first published by McGraw-Hill in 1978.<ref name="ss">{{cite book|last=Farley|first=Lin|title=Sexual Shakedown: The Sexual Harassment of Women on the Job|isbn=0-07-019957-4|url=https://archive.org/details/sexualshakedowns00far_x3q|year=1978|publisher=McGraw-Hill|url-access=registration}}</ref> ''Sexual Shakedown'' inspired the first workplace training video on sexual harassment.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |title=Sexual Shakedown: The Sexual Harassment of Women on the Job, 1978 |url=https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/541410/ |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=The Henry Ford |language=en}}</ref>

=== Legal view ===
The legal understanding of sexual harassment developed through lawsuits women brought forward in the U.S. in the 1970s and 1980s.<ref name=":14" /><ref name="Lipsitz-2017">{{Cite news |last=Lipsitz |first=Raina |date=20 October 2017 |title=Sexual Harassment Law Was Shaped by the Battles of Black Women |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/sexual-harassment-law-was-shaped-by-the-battles-of-black-women/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180408074746/https://www.thenation.com/article/sexual-harassment-law-was-shaped-by-the-battles-of-black-women/ |archive-date=8 April 2018 |access-date=12 April 2018 |work=The Nation |language=en-US |issn=0027-8378}}</ref> The development of U.S. laws on sexual harassment in workplaces shaped similar developments in other countries.<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last1=Earle |first1=Beverley H. |last2=Madek |first2=Gerald A. |date=June 1994 |title=An International Perspective on Sexual Harassment Law |url=https://scholarship.law.umn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1528&context=lawineq |journal=Minnesota Journal of Law & Inequality |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=70–87}}</ref> Many of the women pursuing the earliest U.S. cases were African American, often former civil rights activists, who applied principles of civil rights to sex discrimination.<ref name="Lipsitz-2017" /> Early precedent was set with ''[[Diane R. Williams|Williams]] v. Saxbe'' (1976) and ''[[Barnes v. Train|Paulette L. Barnes, Appellant, v. Douglas M. Costle, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency]]'' (1977) which determined it was sex discrimination to fire someone for refusing a supervisor's advances.<ref name="Lipsitz-2017" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Baker |first=Carrie N. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2wBPD1vvTCYC&q=%22Diane+Williams%22&pg=PA92 |title=The Women's Movement Against Sexual Harassment |date=2008 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-87935-4 |language=en |access-date=4 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230121175236/https://books.google.com/books?id=2wBPD1vvTCYC&q=%22Diane+Williams%22&pg=PA92 |archive-date=21 January 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1979, American legal scholar and activist [[Catharine MacKinnon]] published a seminal book called ''Sexual Harassment of Working Women''.<ref name="U.Mich-2018">{{Cite web |title=MacKinnon, Catharine A. |url=https://www.law.umich.edu/FacultyBio/Pages/FacultyBio.aspx?FacID=camtwo |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411204853/https://www.law.umich.edu/FacultyBio/Pages/FacultyBio.aspx?FacID=camtwo |archive-date=11 April 2018 |access-date=11 April 2018 |website=University of Michigan Law School |language=en-US}}</ref> She popularized the argument that some workplace sexual harassment was consistent with sex discrimination and therefore prohibited behavior under [[Civil Rights Act of 1964|Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964]].<ref>{{cite book |last=MacKinnon |first=Catharine |url=https://archive.org/details/sexualharassment00cath |title=Sexual Harassment of Working Women: A Case of Sex Discrimination. |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-300-02299-5 |location=New Haven, Connecticut |url-access=registration}}</ref> MacKinnon also developed the legal classification of sexual harassment types, as ''quid pro quo'' or hostile environment harassment.<ref name=":5" /> MacKinnon's arguments were key to developing international legal understandings of sexual harassment.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":14" /><ref name=":16" />
[[File:Lesbophobia.png|alt=Illustration of two women embracing in a crowd with one kissing the other. In the background, one person points and another yells at the couple, and people stare in the foreground.|thumb|Harassment regarding [[sexual orientation]], rather than [[gender]] alone, is recognized as a form of sexual harassment under some laws.]]
In the U.S., sexual harassment case law continued soon after with ''[[Bundy v. Jackson]]'' (1981), the first [[United States courts of appeals|federal appeals court]] case to hold that workplace sexual harassment was employment discrimination. Five years later the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] agreed with this holding in ''[[Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson]].''<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mullins |first=Luke |date=4 March 2018 |title=#HerToo: 40 Years Ago This Woman Helped Make Sexual Harassment Illegal |url=https://washingtonian.com/2018/03/04/hertoo-40-years-ago-this-woman-helped-make-sexual-harassment-illegal-sandra-bundy/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180410135537/https://www.washingtonian.com/2018/03/04/hertoo-40-years-ago-this-woman-helped-make-sexual-harassment-illegal-sandra-bundy/ |archive-date=10 April 2018 |access-date=10 April 2018 |work=Washingtonian |language=en-US}}</ref> Another pioneering legal case was ''[[Alexander v. Yale]]'' (1980), which established that the sexual harassment of female students could be considered sex discrimination under [[Title IX]], and was thus illegal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Butler |first=Eric T. |date=2024 |title=Alexander v. Yale: The Transformative Power of Social Forces to Bend Legal Doctrine |url=https://www.nacua.org/docs/default-source/jcul-articles/volume49/butler_titleixyale.pdf?sfvrsn=a16d48be_1 |journal=Journal of College and University Law |volume=49 |issue=1 |page=52}}</ref> The first class-action lawsuit, ''[[Jenson v. Eveleth Taconite Co.]]'', was filed in 1988 (concluding nine years later).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dill |first=Emma |date=26 February 2018 |title=The sexual harassment class-action started at a Minnesota mine that helped set national precedent |url=https://www.minnpost.com/mnopedia/2018/02/sexual-harassment-class-action-started-minnesota-mine-helped-set-national-precedent/ |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=MinnPost |language=en-US}}</ref>

Similar precedents were set throughout the 1980s in the UK based on the [[Sex Discrimination Act 1975|1975 Sex Discrimination Act]].<ref name=":14" /> Throughout the late 1980s, other countries began to establish laws against sexual harassment, and by 1994, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, and Sweden had established laws targeting sexual harassment.<ref name=":17" /> By 2021, 142 countries had laws against sexual harassment in the workplace, with 103 countries prohibiting both ''quid pro quo'' and hostile environment harassment. 39 countries had laws explicitly prohibiting sexual harassment based on sexual orientation, and 24 countries explicitly addressed harassment based on gender identity.<ref name=":15" />

=== Beyond sexual advances ===
Definitions of sexual harassment have changed over time, and common legal definitions now differ in some ways from those used by psychologists and other researchers. All tend to incorporate an element of unwelcome behavior, but researchers often define sexual harassment by the behavior that occurred, while legal definitions focus on whether certain requirements are met.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Fitzgerald |first1=Louise F. |chapter=Sexual harassment in work organizations: A view from the 21st century. |date=2018 |title=APA handbook of the psychology of women: Perspectives on women's private and public lives (Vol. 2). |pages=216–218 |editor-last=Travis |editor-first=Cheryl B |chapter-url=https://content.apa.org/books/16035-012 |access-date=25 July 2025 |place=Washington |publisher=American Psychological Association |language=en |doi=10.1037/0000060-012 |isbn=978-1-4338-2801-0 |last2=Cortina |first2=Lilia M. |editor2-last=White |editor2-first=Jacquelyn W. |editor3-last=Rutherford |editor3-first=Alexandra |editor4-last=Williams |editor4-first=Wendi S.}}</ref>

Over the 1980s and 1990s, psychologists defined ''gender harassment'' as a key subtype of sexual harassment. Gender harassment is a class of verbal or nonverbal behaviors that insult or provoke based on gender: examples include sexual comments or jokes, sexualized imagery, and comments based on gendered stereotypes.<ref name="Fitzgerald-1995" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berdahl |first1=Jennifer L. |last2=Magley |first2=Vicki J. |last3=Waldo |first3=Craig R. |date=1996 |title=The Sexual Harassment of Men? |journal=Psychology of Women Quarterly |volume=20 |pages=531–532 |doi=10.1111/j.1471-6402.1996.tb00320.x |via=Sage Journals}}</ref> Notably, all of these examples were provided in Rowe's original 1973 ''Saturn's Rings'' report on sexual harassment and discrimination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rowe |first=Mary P. |date=December 1973 |title=The Progress of Women in Educational Institutions: The Saturn's Rings Phenomenon |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/155302/Rowe_PA_1973_Saturns-Rings-with-Case-Study.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |journal=Report to MIT Academic Council}}</ref> There are many motivations for gender harassment, but two important ones are sexist beliefs and [[gender policing]]. Both factors cause gender harassment to reinforce existing [[gender role]]s, causing legal scholar [[Katherine Franke]] to label gender harassment as "a technology of sexism".<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Rabelo |first1=Verónica Caridad |last2=Cortina |first2=Lilia M. |date=2014 |title=Two Sides of the Same Coin: Gender Harassment and Heterosexist Harassment in LGBQ Work Lives |journal=Law and Human Behavior |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=379–380|doi=10.1037/lhb0000087 |pmid=24933169 }}</ref>

Gender harassment has nothing to do with sexual attraction and is not a type of sexual advance. This can make it confusing that it is a type of sexual harassment, because the word "sexual" seems to imply underlying sexual desire.<ref name=":1" /> Initial legal and social theories of sexual harassment often viewed it as motivated by sexual desire. However, explanations of the underlying cause later changed to a male desire to dominate or a desire for anyone to maintain their sex-based social status.<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last=Berdahl |first=Jennifer L. |date=April 2007 |title=Harassment Based on Sex: Protecting Social Status in the Context of Gender Hierarchy |url=https://www-2.rotman.utoronto.ca/facBios/file/BerdahlAMR2007.pdf |journal=Academy of Management Review |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=641–644 |doi=10.5465/amr.2007.24351879 }}</ref> These theories reframe sexual harassment as harassment based on sex or gender, rather than something inherently sexual. Various legal and sociological definitions of sexual harassment include non-sexual, sexist behavior, but the emphasis on the word "sexual" means the definitions often cause confusion and debate.<ref name=":18" /><ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Saguy |first1=Abigail C. |last2=Rees |first2=Mallory E. |date=31 July 2021 |title=Gender, Power, and Harassment: Sociology in the #MeToo Era |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-soc-090320-031147 |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |language=en |volume=47 |issue= |pages=417–435 |doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-090320-031147 |issn=0360-0572}}</ref> Some laws explicitly cover unwanted sexual and sex-based behavior under their definition of "sexual harassment," while others define sex-based harassment and sexual harassment as two different types of harassment.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 March 2011 |title=Overview and Definition |url=https://www.endvawnow.org/en/articles/817-overview-and-definition.html |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=UN Women – Virtual Knowledge Center to End Violence against Women and Girls}}</ref> Some researchers have advocated for the term "sexual harassment" to be replaced with "sex-based harassment" to emphasize the fact that these types of harassment center on gender, not the presence of sexual desire in harassment.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":19" />

In the late 1990s, some legal scholars began to advocate for more explicitly including gender harassment in sexual harassment law, but this was a minority view.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leskinen |first1=Emily A. |last2=Cortina |first2=Lilia M. |last3=Kabat |first3=Dana M. |date=2010 |title=Gender Harassment: Broadening Our Understanding of Sex-Based Harassment at Work |journal=Law and Human Behavior |volume=35 |issue=1|pages=25–39 |doi=10.1007/s10979-010-9241-5 |pmid=20661766 }}</ref> Existing sexual harassment law frequently does cover some instances of gender harassment, but it is often viewed as less severe than other types of sexual harassment in a legal context. However, psychologists continue to emphasize the study of gender harassment because it is by far the most common type of harassment and has major negative consequences both for the individuals faced with it and the groups who are exposed to repeated gender harassment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=Sharon K. |last2=Griffin |first2=Mark A. |date=2002 |title=What Is So Bad About a Little Name-Calling? Negative Consequences of Gender Harassment for Overperformance Demands and Distress |url=https://doi.org/10.1037//1076-8998.7.3.195 |journal=Journal of Occupational Health Psychology |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=195–196|doi=10.1037/1076-8998.7.3.195 |pmid=12148952 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Aspects ==
[[File:ExecutingAWrit.png|alt=A large man dressed in a top hat and holding a briefcase holds a chair and watching a woman as she undresses.|thumb|Quid pro quo exchange illustrated in a lithograph created around 1912 called "Executing a writ: so like this I don't owe any rent?"]]
There is no universal definition of sexual harassment: understandings of it vary across legal, scientific, and cultural settings.<ref name=":12" /> Social scientists define sexual harassment by the type of behavior involved and its effect on victims. By these definitions, sexual harassment includes hostile sexist acts (gender harassment), unwanted sexual attention, and sexual coercion.<ref name=":7" /> Legal definitions of workplace sexual harassment tend to classify it into ''quid pro quo'' demands for sexual favors in exchange for job impacts, or offensive conduct that creates a hostile environment. Laws differ on whether both are considered illegal sexual harassment and whether sexual harassment includes only sexually-related harassment or also harassment based on gender.<ref name=":15" />

Sexual harassment also includes other types, examples can be making sexual comments or jokes, touching someone without their consent, [[indecent exposure]]<ref name="McDonald"/> and sending unwanted messages. Actions like this can make people feel uncomfortable or even disrespected. Because of things like this, a lot of workplaces have created policies to prevent sexual harassment and also to help people report it.<ref name=":23" />

=== Labeling as sexual harassment ===
One of the difficulties in understanding sexual harassment is that it involves a range of [[behavior]]s. In most cases (although not in all cases), it is difficult for the victim to describe what they experienced. This can be related to difficulty classifying the situation, or to [[stress (biology)|stress]] and [[humiliation]] experienced by the recipient. Moreover, behavior and motives vary between individual cases.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Louise |first=Fitzgerald |year=1995 |title=Why Didn't She Just Report Him? The Psychological and Legal Implications of Women's Responses to Sexual Harassment |journal=Journal of Social Issues |volume=51 |pages=117–138 |doi=10.1111/j.1540-4560.1995.tb01312.x}}</ref>

Many instances of sexual harassment are not actually labeled that way by the involved parties. For female victims of experiences that match social science definitions of sexual harassment, victims only self-label the experience as sexual harassment 25% of the time. The rate is even lower for male victims. However, whether victims label an incident as sexual harassment or not, they report the same levels of distress and negative impact.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Cortina |first1=Lilia M. |last2=Areguin |first2=Maira A. |date=2021 |title=Putting People Down and Pushing Them Out: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/liliacortina-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/970/2021/12/Cortina-Areguin-2021-Annual-Review.pdf |journal=Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior |volume=8 |pages=294–295|doi=10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-055606 }}</ref> This labeling issue was first discovered after other researchers found that victims of rape are similarly unlikely to label their experience as rape.<ref name=":4" />

Many contextual factors affect how likely people are to label an incident as sexual harassment, and the power dynamics between the perpetrator and victim are a key influence on people's perceptions. People's labeling decisions are also correlated with their gender and relationship to gender roles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bursik |first1=Krisanne |last2=Gefter |first2=Julia |date=21 April 2011 |title=Still Stable After All These Years: Perceptions of Sexual Harassment in Academic Contexts |journal=The Journal of Social Psychology |volume=151 |issue=3 |page=333 |doi=10.1080/00224541003628081 |issn=0022-4545 |pmid=21675185}}</ref> During the 1990s and 2000s, women who self-labeled their experiences as sexual harassment were often derided as too sensitive or aiming to make trouble, in addition to being questioned about misinterpreting the harassment, especially if it could be claimed to be unintentional behavior. One 2001 analysis found that women often self-labeled their experiences of unwanted gendered and sexual behavior as "sexism" or the product of a "sexualized environment" rather than sexual harassment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lazard |first1=Lisa |last2=Capdevila |first2=Rose |last3=Turner |first3=Jim |date=2025 |title=Calling it out? A Q Methodological Study of Sexual Harassment Labelling |journal=Violence Against Women |language=en |volume=31 |issue=1 |page=331 |doi=10.1177/10778012231209011 |issn=1077-8012 |pmc=11610199 |pmid=37880954}}</ref>

In some cases visible [[Cleavage (breasts)|cleavage]] have been labeled as sexual harassment.<ref name="McDonald">{{Cite journal |last1=McDonald |first1=Paula |last2=Charlesworth |first2=Sara |date=2016 |title=Workplace sexual harassment at the margins |journal=Work, Employment and Society |language=EN |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=118–134 |doi=10.1177/0950017014564615 |issn=0950-0170}}</ref>

=== Types of sexual harassment ===
Scientists commonly classify types of sexual harassment via Fitzgerald's Tripartite Model of Sexual Harassment, which has been validated across gender, ethnicity, nation, and industry. The model divides sexual harassment into gender harassment, unwanted sexual attention, and sexual coercion.<ref name=":7" />
[[File:AFIS BILLBOARD POSTERS. COOL NAMES FOR WOMEN? SEXUAL HARASSMENT AWARENESS. DEFENSE BILLBOARD -49 DD-SC-00-02339.jpg|alt=A poster of a fox in a snowy field with an overlaid image of a chick and a doll, with the captions: "COOL NAMES FOR WOMEN?" "THE COLD FACTS: THEY'RE NOT!" |thumb|Poster against calling women sexualized names as part of an anti-sexual harassment campaign by [[American Forces Information Service|AFIS]] in 2000.]]
Gender harassment includes insults based on gender stereotypes, sexual slurs or imagery, and other degrading or hostile communications that aim to "put people down and push them out" due to their sex.<ref name=":7" /> There are two types of gender harassment: sexist hostility, like insulting gendered jokes, insults based on gender stereotypes, or even sabotage; and crude harassment, which includes gendered slurs and sexualized insults.<ref name=":4" /> In contrast, unwanted sexual attention refers to unwelcome sexual advances, like inappropriately talking about sex, pestering someone for sexual or romantic purposes, non-consensual physical touch, and, in extreme cases, sexual assault. Sexual coercion includes explicit and implicit attempts to bribe or threaten someone into sexual cooperation.<ref name=":7" />

Gender harassment is by far the most common type of sexual harassment, and coercion is the rarest. Still, popular awareness of harassment is the opposite, making it harder to identify and understand sexual harassment. Psychology researcher Lilia Cortina developed an iceberg model to describe the many behaviors of sexual harassment, showing how sexual coercion and unwanted sexual attention are the small set of harassment behaviors easily viewable on the surface, but the vast majority of sexual harassment types lie underneath the surface in the category of gender harassment.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Cortina |first1=Lilia M. |last2=Areguin |first2=Maira A. |date=2021 |title=Putting People Down and Pushing Them Out: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/liliacortina-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/970/2021/12/Cortina-Areguin-2021-Annual-Review.pdf |journal=Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior |volume=8 |pages=287–288, 294|doi=10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-055606 }}</ref>

=== Intersectional forms of sexual harassment ===
When women of color are sexually harassed, it often includes racial harassment, and when non-straight women are harassed, it often is a combination of sexual and heterosexist harassment. Both populations experience much greater harassment than people with only one of their intersecting identities.<ref name=":4" /> Racialized sexual harassment may involve sexual remarks that also bring up race, pet names with racial histories, or even explicitly racialized nicknames. All of these may be built off of existing stereotypes that combine race and gender.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cortina |first1=Lilia M. |last2=Areguin |first2=Maira A. |date=2021 |title=Putting People Down and Pushing Them Out: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/liliacortina-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/970/2021/12/Cortina-Areguin-2021-Annual-Review.pdf |journal=Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior |volume=8 |page=301|doi=10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-055606 }}</ref>

When men sexually harass men, it tends to take the form of gender harassment for the purpose of punishing their targets for deviating from traditional male [[gender role]]s. The harasser may see their victim as not fulfilling traditional [[masculinity]] values, whether they are gay, young, or inexperienced.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cortina |first1=Lilia M. |last2=Areguin |first2=Maira A. |date=2021 |title=Putting People Down and Pushing Them Out: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/liliacortina-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/970/2021/12/Cortina-Areguin-2021-Annual-Review.pdf |journal=Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior |volume=8 |page=292 |doi=10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-055606}}</ref> Women harassing men is reported less frequently than men harassing women.<ref name="McDonald"/>

==== Women of color ====
[[File:Montevideo libre de acoso (campaña).jpg|alt=Outdoor mural in progress, with a starry night sky in the background and a Black woman with makeup and jewelry looking back at the viewer. Below, the words "TRANSITEMOS LIBRES de ACOSO" are painted.|thumb|Mural painted for the "[[Montevideo]] free of harassment" campaign.]]
The sexual harassment [[women of color]] face is often ignored when discussions about the sexual harassment women face occur.<ref name="Welsh-2006">{{Cite journal |last1=Welsh |first1=Sandy |last2=Carr |first2=Jacquie |last3=MacQuarrie |first3=Barbara |last4=Huntley |first4=Audrey |date=2006 |title="I'm Not Thinking of It as Sexual Harassment": Understanding Harassment across Race and Citizenship |journal=Gender and Society |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=87–107 |doi=10.1177/0891243205282785 |jstor=27640867 |s2cid=145101291 |issn=0891-2432 }}</ref> Harassment of women of color tends to stem from [[racial discrimination]].<ref name="Welsh-2006"/> Poor African American women are more likely to experience sexual harassment but less likely to be seen as a victim.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Buchanan |first1=Nicole T. |last2=Ormerod |first2=Alayne J. |date=29 October 2002 |title=Racialized Sexual Harassment in the Lives of African American Women |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1300/J015v25n03_08 |journal=Women & Therapy |language=en |volume=25 |issue=3–4 |pages=107–124 |doi=10.1300/J015v25n03_08 |s2cid=144425126 |issn=0270-3149 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518022534/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1300/J015v25n03_08 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stockdale |first=Margaret |date=1996 |title=Sexual Harassment in the Workplace: Perspectives, Frontiers, and Response Strategies |doi=10.4135/9781483327280 |isbn=978-0-8039-5794-7 |url=https://sk.sagepub.com/books/sexual-harassment-in-the-workplace|access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518022535/https://sk.sagepub.com/books/sexual-harassment-in-the-workplace |url-status=live }}</ref> Conditions like these make it difficult for women of color to report sexual harassment, allowing the cycle to continue.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Feagin |first=Joe R. |date=1992 |title=On Not Taking Gendered Racism Seriously: The Failure of the Mass Media and the Social Sciences |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0021886392283007 |journal=The Journal of Applied Behavioral Science |language=en |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=400–406 |doi=10.1177/0021886392283007 |s2cid=144210172 |issn=0021-8863 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=7 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407001052/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0021886392283007 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Earlier studies revealed that there was no difference between the sexual harassment rates of white women and women of color.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=26 September 1997 |title=Sexual Harassment in the Federal Workplace: 1978-1980, 1987, and 1994 |website=ICPSR Data Holdings |doi=10.3886/icpsr06893.v1 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Crosby |first=Faye J. |date=1987 |title=Sex and the Workplace: The Impact of Sexual Behavior and Harassment on Women, Men, and Organizations, by Barbara A. Gutek. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 1985. 216pp. (xv). $19.95 hard cover. |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/036168438701100101 |journal=Psychology of Women Quarterly |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=130–132 |doi=10.1177/036168438701100101 |s2cid=146819853 |issn=0361-6843 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=6 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230606161929/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/036168438701100101 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, evidence suggests that women of color experience sexual harassment on more severe terms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gruber |first1=James E. |last2=Bjorn |first2=Lars |date=1982 |title=Blue-Collar Blues: The Sexual Harassment of Women Autoworkers |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0730888482009003002 |journal=Work and Occupations |language=en |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=271–298 |doi=10.1177/0730888482009003002 |s2cid=143586619 |issn=0730-8884 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=7 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407001059/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0730888482009003002 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Welsh |first=Sandy |date=1999 |title=Gender and Sexual Harassment |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/199590842 |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |volume=25 |pages=169–190 |doi=10.1146/annurev.soc.25.1.169 |id={{ProQuest|199590842}} |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=20 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020130956/https://www.proquest.com/docview/199590842 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Race and gender influence most of the sexual harassment that women of color face. Women of color are less likely to report sexual harassment if the perpetrator is of the same race. This is known as the code of silence. The race of the harasser influences this and predominantly affects women of color.<ref name="Richardson-2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Richardson |first1=Brian K. |last2=Taylor |first2=Juandalynn |date=4 August 2009 |title=Sexual Harassment at the Intersection of Race and Gender: A Theoretical Model of the Sexual Harassment Experiences of Women of Color |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10570310903082065 |journal=Western Journal of Communication |language=en |volume=73 |issue=3 |pages=248–272 |doi=10.1080/10570310903082065 |s2cid=143660626 |issn=1057-0314 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=14 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314025838/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10570310903082065 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Black women do not usually see things that a white woman would claim to be sexual harassment because they are accustomed to it, it is normal to them and so there is not much of a problem.<ref name="Welsh-2006"/>

Something unique to the sexual harassment of women of color is the common bond factor. The common bond factor is when a man of color sees someone of their own race or culture, and they feel as if it is okay to harass them sexually. They think they can act and speak without regard for the law because they feel it is not being broken.<ref name="Richardson-2009"/>

The perception of sexual harassment from women of color includes racism and sexism, whereas white women's perception only includes sexism. There is this interlocking of relations, commonly known as [[intersectionality]], within the sexual harassment women of color face, between racism and sexism. White women, when speaking about sexual harassment, speak from the role of a victim, whereas women of color speak from the role of a harasser. Women of color, as well, have stereotypes taken into consideration when it comes to harassment. These stereotypes make it difficult for women of color to come forward about sexual harassment, as they will likely not be believed.<ref name="Richardson-2009"/> For instance, there is the stereotype that Latin women are super emotional and tend to overreact. This stereotype may be conveyed when a Latina woman comes forward about sexual harassment, resulting in her claim not being taken seriously. Speaking up results in stereotypes being put on the person coming forward, making them uncomfortable with doing so.<ref name="Richardson-2009" /> Similarly, it is difficult for women of color to be supported when speaking out, as their experiences are different from those of white women, as is the case with Anita Hill.<ref name="Pantheon Books-1992">{{Cite book |title=Race-ing justice, en-gendering power: essays on Anita Hill, Clarence Thomas, and the construction of social reality |date=1992 |publisher=Pantheon Books |others=Toni Morrison |isbn=0-679-74145-3 |edition=1 |location=New York |oclc=25632335 }}</ref> Particularly, the feminist movement is geared towards helping white women rather than women of color due to women of color's experiences being foreign. In turn, women of color do not join feminist movements or groups because they do not see their experiences reflected.<ref name="Pantheon Books-1992" />

There is a relationship between legal status and sexual harassment; there is an [[intersectionality]] between them. Citizen status can influence women experiencing or reporting sexual harassment. Being undocumented can make it difficult to come forward for fear of being deported.<ref name="Welsh-2006"/> White women with citizenship say that sexual harassment is unwanted behavior, women of color without citizenship found it difficult to explain what they thought sexual harassment was, but that it did include race.<ref name="Welsh-2006" /> This, however, makes it difficult for Black women to differentiate sexual harassment in the workplace from sexual harassment in society.<ref name="Welsh-2006" />

=== Motivations for sexual harassment ===
Author Martha Langelan describes four different classes of harassers.<ref>Langelan, Martha. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=laA-lkQq8soC Back Off: How to Confront and Stop Sexual Harassment and Harassers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160105082011/https://books.google.com/books?id=laA-lkQq8soC&printsec=frontcover |date=5 January 2016 }}''. Fireside, 1993. {{ISBN|978-0-671-78856-8}}.</ref>
[[File:Ilustrasi Catcalling.png|alt=An illustration of two black cats smiling and saying something to a person who turns and angrily yells back at them.|thumb|Portrayal of [[catcalling]], a common form of [[street harassment]].]]
* A predatory harasser: a person who gets sexual thrills from humiliating others. This harasser may become involved in sexual extortion and may frequently harass just to see how targets respond. Those who do not resist may even become targets for rape.
* A dominance harasser: the most common type, who engages in harassing behavior as an ego boost.
* Strategic or territorial harassers who seek to maintain privilege in jobs or physical locations, for example, a man's harassment of a female employee in a predominantly male occupation.
* A [[Street harassment|street harasser]]: Another type of sexual harassment performed in public places by strangers. Street harassment includes verbal and nonverbal behavior, remarks that are frequently sexual in nature, and comments on physical appearance or a person's presence in public.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Street Harassment and the Informal Ghettoization of Women |first=Cynthia Grant |last=Bowman |journal=Harvard Law Review |volume=106 |issue=3 |date=Jan 1993 |pages=517–80 |jstor=1341656 |doi=10.2307/1341656 |url=https://scholarship.law.cornell.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1141&context=facpub |access-date=4 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109090954/http://scholarship.law.cornell.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1141&context=facpub |archive-date=9 January 2020 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
The perpetrators of sexual harassment are more likely to be male than female. In one 2018 survey of U.S. federal workers who were asked to recall the most distressing times they had been sexually harassed, 82% of the harassers were men. Researchers theorize that men are more likely to sexually harass because it is an expression of power that strengthens the harasser's gender-based social status. Because today's societies empower men over people of other genders, sexual harassment is most effective at reinforcing the social privileges of men.<ref name=":20" />

This power-based theory of harassment also explains why sexual harassment often targets and punishes people for deviating from traditional gender roles. People are more likely to sexually harass when they hold hostile, sexist beliefs and believe in the [[gender binary]], thinking that men and women should stay in certain proper roles. However, whether they actually harass others strongly depends on the situation: organizations that tolerate or do not care about harassment, and places that prioritize men by numbers or leadership are very likely to have sexual harassment occur.<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Cortina |first1=Lilia M. |last2=Areguin |first2=Maira A. |date=2021 |title=Putting People Down and Pushing Them Out: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/liliacortina-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/970/2021/12/Cortina-Areguin-2021-Annual-Review.pdf |journal=Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior |volume=8 |pages=287, 292, 295–296|doi=10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-055606 }}</ref>

Sexual harassment's usefulness in reinforcing power and gender roles shapes how it occurs. Even when harassment seems to express a harasser's sexual desire, it is often motivated by the desire to punish someone for not conforming to gender roles or to devalue women due to their gender. Harassment is often ambient: not targeted at an individual but public or pervasive within a setting, affecting many bystanders. Even targeted harassment can affect other observers when it occurs publicly.<ref name=":4" />

==Situations==
[[File:Berthold Woltze - Der lästige Kavalier.jpg|alt=Painting of a woman dressed in black with a floral bag on a train bench. Behind her, a man in grey leans over the bench to smile and talk at her, holding up his spectacles to see her. She looks away from him, straight at the painting's viewer, frowning.|thumb|1874 painting by B. Woltze Weimar portraying a man sexually harassing a woman in mourning on a train.]]
Sexual harassment may occur in a variety of circumstances and in places as varied as factories, schools, colleges, the theater, and the music business.<ref>{{cite news|last=Philips|first=Chuck|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-04-18-ca-24123-story.html|title=Cover Story: You've Still Got a Long Way to Go, Baby|date=18 April 1993|newspaper=Los |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PKG5er5AnBkC&q=Chuck+Philips+sexual+harassment&pg=PA113 |access-date=4 October 2020 |archive-date=21 January 2023 or is about to have [[Power (social and political)|power]] or authority over the victim (owing to differences in social, political, educational or employment relationships as well as in age). Harassment relationships are specified in many ways:
* The perpetrator can be anyone, such as a client, a partner, a co-worker, a parent or legal guardian, a relative, a teacher or professor, a student, a friend, or a stranger.
* Harassment can occur in varying locations, in schools,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sior.ub.edu/jspui/cris/socialimpact/socialimpact00415|title=Reporting of violence against women in University. [Social Impact]. VGU. Gender-based Violence in Spanish Universities (2006–2008).|date=2017|website=SIOR, Social Impact Open Repository|publisher=Universitat de Barcelona|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180718030651/http://sior.ub.edu/jspui/cris/socialimpact/socialimpact00415|archive-date=18 July 2018}}</ref> colleges, workplaces, in public, and in other places.
* Harassment can occur whether or not there are witnesses to it.
* The perpetrator may be completely unaware that their behavior is offensive or constitutes sexual harassment. The perpetrator may be completely unaware that their actions could be unlawful.<ref name="eeoc" />
* Incidents of harassment can take place in situations in which the targeted person may not be aware of or understand what is happening.
* An incident may be a one-time occurrence.
* Adverse effects on harassed persons include stress, social withdrawal, sleep disorders, eating difficulties, and other impairments of health.
* The victim and perpetrator can be any gender.
* The incident may arise from a misunderstanding by the perpetrator and/or the victim. These misunderstandings can be reasonable or unreasonable.
* The perpetrator may be motivated by many things, including wanting to belittle, embarrass, or intimidate the victim because of their sex, or in wanting to express sexual desire<ref>{{Cite web |title=Questions and Answers for Employees: Harassment at Work |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/questions-and-answers-employees-harassment-work |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |language=en}}</ref> 
[[File:Online harassment of women journalists.png|alt=Graphic of a woman sitting behind a computer covering her face, surrounded by icons captioned: cyber-stalking, doxxing, trolling, cyber-bullying, hate speech, public shaming, and intimidation/threats.|thumb|Examples of [[online harassment]] commonly experienced by women journalists, who face higher levels of harassment, in more gendered and sexual forms, than men in those roles.<ref>{{Cite book |title=World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development Global Report 2017/2018 |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |year=2018 |isbn=978-92-3-100242-7 |pages=155–157 |language=}}</ref>]]
With the advent of the internet, social interactions, including sexual harassment, increasingly occur online, for example, [[sexual harassment in video gaming|in video games]] or in chat rooms.

According to the 2014 PEW research statistics on online harassment, 25% of women and 13% of men between the ages of 18 and 24 have experienced sexual harassment while online.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2014/10/22/online-harassment/|title=Online Harassment|last=Duggan|first=Maeve|date=22 October 2014|website=Pew Research Center|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201015535/https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2014/10/22/online-harassment/|archive-date=1 February 2020|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

=== In the workplace ===
{{Further|Sexual harassment in education|Sexual harassment in the workplace in the United States}}

The United States' [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]] (EEOC) defines workplace sexual harassment as harassment based on a victim's sex, including "offensive remarks about a person's sex" or "unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature".<ref name="eeoc" /> Harassment is illegal "when this conduct explicitly or implicitly affects an individual's employment, unreasonably interferes with an individual's work performance, or creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment".<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 January 1997 |title=Fact Sheet: Sexual Harassment Discrimination |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/fact-sheet-sexual-harassment-discrimination |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |language=en}}</ref> "The challenged conduct must be unwelcome in the sense that the employee did not solicit or incite it, and in the sense that the employee regarded the conduct as undesirable or offensive."<ref name="unwelcome">{{cite web |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/policy-guidance-current-issues-sexual-harassment |title=Policy Guidance on Current Issues of Sexual Harassment |author=<!--Not stated--> |website= |date=19 March 1990 |publisher=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |access-date=6 August 2021 |quote= |archive-date=5 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605132047/https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/policy-guidance-current-issues-sexual-harassment |url-status=live }}</ref> "Particularly when the alleged harasser may have some reason (e.g., prior consensual relationship) to believe that the advances will be welcomed, it is important for the victim to communicate that the conduct is unwelcome."<ref name="unwelcome" />

Surveys vary widely in determining how frequently sexual harassment occurs in workplaces. A well-regarded 2003 meta-survey concluded that about 58% of women have been sexually harassed at work.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/24994 |title=Sexual Harassment of Women: Climate, Culture, and Consequences in Academic Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |publisher=National Academies Press |others=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine: Committee on the Impacts of Sexual Harassment in Academia; Committee on Women in Science, Engineering, and Medicine; Policy and Global Affairs |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-309-47087-2 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Paula A. |location=Washington, D.C. |doi=10.17226/24994 |bibcode=2018nap..book24994N |editor-last2=Widnall |editor-first2=Sheila E. |editor-last3=Benya |editor-first3=Frazier F.}}</ref> Another survey concluded that 13% of male employees have been harassed at work.{{citation needed|date=March 2025}} In a 2024 study, 42% of transgender employees reported having been sexually harassed at work.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 2024 |title=Workplace Experiences of Transgender Employees |url=https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/transgender-workplace-discrim/ |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=UCLA School of Law Williams Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> Women made 78.2% of the workplace sexual harassment complaints filed with the EEOC from 2018 to 2021.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Sexual Harassment in Our Nation's Workplaces |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/data/sexual-harassment-our-nations-workplaces#_ftn2 |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |language=en}}</ref> Only about 30% of workplace sexual harassment victims tell their supervisor or union representative about the harassment. Only 6–13% ever file a formal complaint. Managers often relabel sexual harassment claims as mere interpersonal disagreements, and retaliation is common.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Feldblum |first1=Chai R. |last2=Lipnic |first2=Victoria A. |date=June 2016 |title=Select Task Force on the Study of Harassment in the Workplace |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/select-task-force-study-harassment-workplace#_ftn65 |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |language=en}}</ref> Thus, 43.5% of EEOC sexual harassment complaints included retaliation complaints in 2018–2021.<ref name=":2" /> A survey of harassment case plaintiffs found that 24% had been fired for complaining of harassment, and another 42% had resigned due to the harassment.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Gregory |first=Raymond F. |title=Unwelcome and Unlawful: Sexual Harassment in the American Workplace |publisher=Cornell University Press |year=2018 |location=Ithaca |page=157}}</ref>

Most workplace sexual harassment is perpetrated by coworkers or peers rather than managers. Workplace culture is one of the strongest determining factors for sexual harassment: sexual harassment is more likely in fields that are seen as traditionally masculine, or companies where men outnumber women, or leadership is dominated by men. Organizational tolerance of harassment, sexism, or alcohol use, and institutions with strong power hierarchies, also increase the likelihood of harassment.<ref name=":4" /> Based on data from the EEOC, the industries with the most sexual harassment reports between 2005 and 2015 were restaurant and hospitality, health care, academia, and the military. Sources of harassment vary widely by industry. For nurses, 58% have been harassed by a patient, 26% by a colleague, and 19% by a patient's acquaintances. In the U.S. military, 60% of sexual harassment is caused by a supervisor.{{citation needed|date=March 2025}} For restaurant industry employees, around 66% of women and 50% of men have been sexually harassed by management, and around 80% of women and 55% of men have been sexually harassed by customers.<ref>The Restaurant Opportunities Centers United Forward Together. (2024). ''[https://www.scribd.com/document/242133572/The-Glass-Floor-Sexual-Harassment-in-the-Restaurant-Industry The Glass Floor: Sexual Harassment in the Restaurant Industry]''. Retrieved 13 January 2025.</ref>

Most sexual harassment at work takes the form of gender harassment. A far smaller number of harassment victims report experiencing sexual coercion at work: this was about 4% of women surveyed across factory settings and academia in 1997. Workplace sexual harassment is frequently repeated, with less than a third of victims describing harassment as a one-time occurrence, and many stating it had lasted for weeks to months.<ref name=":4" /> Whether sexual harassment incidents include physical harassment usually depends on the industry: around 50% of sexual harassment complaints by blue-collar workers included a physical component, compared to 32% of complaints by managers. A study of harassment cases in 1986-1995 found that more than half of the instances of workplace harassment occurred entirely outside the workplace, with a third involving letters, phone calls, or visits to the victim's home.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gregory |first=Raymond F. |title=Unwelcome and Unlawful: Sexual Harassment in the American Workplace |publisher=Cornell University Press |year=2018 |location=Ithaca |pages=28, 78}}</ref>

{{See also|Anita Hill|Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination}}
[[File:"I Believe Anita Hill" Button.jpg|thumb|upright=.90|An "I Believe Anita Hill" pin in support of [[Anita Hill]]'s 1991 testimony to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]], where she accused [[Supreme Court of the United States|U.S. Supreme Court]] nominee [[Clarence Thomas]] of sexual harassment]]
In 1991, [[Anita Hill]] witnessed and testified to the [[United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary|Senate Judiciary Committee]] against [[Supreme Court of the United States]] nominee [[Clarence Thomas]], citing sexual harassment.<ref name="techrep">Bowers, Toni; Hook, Brian. [http://www.techrepublic.com/article/hostile-work-environment-a-managers-legal-liability/5035282 Hostile work environment: A manager's legal liability] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160710203301/http://www.techrepublic.com/article/hostile-work-environment-a-managers-legal-liability/5035282/ |date=10 July 2016 }}, Tech Republic. 22 October 2002. Retrieved on 3 March 2012.</ref> Hill said on 11 October 1991, in televised hearings that Thomas had sexually harassed her while he was her supervisor at the Department of Education and the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|EEOC]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Anita Hill's Testimony and Other Key Moments From the Clarence Thomas Hearings |work=The New York Times |date=20 September 2018 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/20/us/politics/anita-hill-testimony-clarence-thomas.html |access-date=15 July 2022 |archive-date=29 December 2021 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20211229221215/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/20/us/politics/anita-hill-testimony-clarence-thomas.html |url-status=bot: unknown |last1=Jacobs |first1=Julia }}</ref> According to Hill, Thomas asked her out socially many times during her two years of employment as his assistant,<ref name="Suro">{{Cite news |last=Suro |first=Roberto |date=8 October 1991 |title=The Thomas Nomination – A Law Professor Defends Integrity |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/08/us/the-thomas-nomination-a-law-professor-defends-integrity.html |access-date=15 July 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=27 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181127022630/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/08/us/the-thomas-nomination-a-law-professor-defends-integrity.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and after she declined his requests, he used work situations to discuss sexual subjects and push advances.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.gpoaccess.gov/congress/senate/judiciary/sh102-1084pt4/41-124.pdf |access-date=15 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111107034024/http://www.gpoaccess.gov/congress/senate/judiciary/sh102-1084pt4/41-124.pdf |archive-date=7 November 2011|title=Testimony of Anita Hill }}</ref><ref name="Suro"/> Since Hill testified in 1991, the term ''sexual harassment'' became known outside academic and legal circles; the number of cases reported in the United States and Canada increased markedly, climbing steadily since.<ref name="techrep" /> Sexual harassment is discussed a lot in modern society. People are becoming more and more concerned about the laws of sexual harassment therein. Many school groups are focusing on this matter.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pilgaard |first1=Frida |last2=Agardh |first2=Anette |last3=Östergren |first3=Per-Olof |last4=Priebe |first4=Gisela |date=20 December 2022 |title=Association between Experiences of Different Types of Harassment or Derogatory Treatment and Sexual Harassment among Employees at a Large Swedish University |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |volume=20 |issue=1 |page=11 |doi=10.3390/ijerph20010011 |pmid=36612332 |pmc=9819109 |issn=1660-4601 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
{{See also|Paula Jones|Bill Clinton sexual assault and misconduct allegations}}

In 1994, [[Paula Jones]], a civil servant and former Arkansas state employee, sued President [[Bill Clinton]] for sexual harassment. In the initial lawsuit, Jones cited Clinton for sexual harassment at a hotel in 1991. Following a series of civil suits and appeals, the case was settled in 1998. President Clinton reached an out-of-court settlement with Jones, agreeing to pay her $850,000 but acknowledging no wrongdoing.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Washingtonpost.com: Jones v. Clinton Special Report |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/special/pjones/timeline.htm |access-date=15 July 2022 |newspaper=The Washington Post |archive-date=12 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180912124457/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/special/pjones/timeline.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Sexual bribery====
A sexual bribe is the solicitation of sex, any sexual activity, or other sex-linked behavior for a promise of elevation in work status or pay. It is in an employment setting in which a sexual relationship with an employer or superior is made an explicit or implied condition for obtaining or retaining employment or its benefits. A sexual bribe may be either overt or subtle but falls under the type of [[quid pro quo]] sexual harassment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjarnegård |first1=Elin |last2=Calvo |first2=Dolores |last3=Eldén |first3=Åsa |last4=Jonsson |first4=Sofia |last5=Lundgren |first5=Silje |title=Sex instead of money: Conceptualizing sexual corruption |journal=Governance |date=October 2024 |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=1349–1367 |doi=10.1111/gove.12844}}</ref>

==== Girl watching ====

Girl watching is considered a game amongst men in which they sexually evaluate women. This game is a form of sexual harassment, one that is very common in the workplace.<ref name="Quinn-2002b">{{Cite journal |last=Quinn |first=Beth A. |date=2002 |title=Sexual Harassment and Masculinity: The Power and Meaning of "Girl Watching" |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243202016003007 |journal=Gender & Society |language=en |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=386–402 |doi=10.1177/0891243202016003007 |s2cid=145230013 |issn=0891-2432 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=7 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407061826/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243202016003007 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This game, just like other forms of sexual harassment are not the actions of an individual outside of the norm, but rather of those within it.<ref name="Messner-2016"/> An analysis of sexual harassment surveys, conducted by Ilies, revealed that when the question regarding sexual harassment was phrased 'if women had ever experienced sexual harassment' then the frequency of women's responses was 24%, whereas if women were asked 'if they had experienced sexually harassing behaviors' then the frequency was 58%.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Remus |last=Ilies |title=Reported incidence rates of work-related sexual harassment in the United States: using meta-analysis to explain reported rate disparities. |date=1 September 2003 |publisher=Personnel Psychology, Inc |oclc=926296251 }}</ref>
[[File:Hentikan Catcalling!!.jpg|alt=A woman wearing a dress sweats as she watches her phone, walking by a group of three men who whistle and laugh at her. One waves, saying "cuit...cuit 'somse' deh sini lah sama kyla!". Another says "Cantik banget neng!" The men smoke and bottles of liquor rest near them. A cat in a box nearby thinks "garong bet luh 3!!"|thumb|Indonesian illustration of a group of men catcalling a woman.]]
Beth Quinn (2002), the author of "Sexual Harassment and Masculinity: The Power and Meaning of 'Girl Watching{{' "}} originally was not researching girl watching when she stumbled upon the game, however, Quinn (2002) stated that her work was more exploratory than confirmatory, explaining why she continued exploring the idea of Girl Watching.<ref name="Quinn-2002b" /> At first, Quinn was researching the difference between what women and men see as sexual harassment. It was through the [[interview]]s (43) that she conducted that she noticed an occurrence of the game in her interviews with men. In addition to conducting interviews, Quinn (2002) [[Observation|observed]] the participants and gathered additional information about the game. She learned that men, usually when in a group, will watch the women around them and make comments towards them.<ref name="Quinn-2002b" />

Quinn (2002) found that men saw no problem with this and viewed it as a game that did no harm to women. According to Quinn, men can excuse sexual harassment because it is not seen as such to them; men see it as a 'game' or 'playing'.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Kristin |last=Bumiller |title=In an Abusive State: How Neoliberalism Appropriated the Feminist Movement against Sexual Violence. |date=2009 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-8907-1 |oclc=1058328198 }}</ref><ref name="Armstrong-2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Armstrong |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Gleckman-Krut |first2=Miriam |last3=Johnson |first3=Lanora |date=30 July 2018 |title=Silence, Power, and Inequality: An Intersectional Approach to Sexual Violence |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |language=en |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=99–122 |doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-073117-041410 |s2cid=150083345 |issn=0360-0572|doi-access=free }}</ref> Men, as well, use humor to harass women sexually. Through humor, men can make crude remarks, and if caught, can claim that it was only a joke and that women need to loosen up. This results in the continuation of sexual harassment against women.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deegan |first=Mary Jo |date=2014 |title=Goffman on Gender, Sexism, and Feminism: A Summary of Notes on a Conversation with Erving Goffman and My Reflections Then and Now |journal=Symbolic Interaction |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=71–86|doi=10.1002/symb.85 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Through instances like these, men sexually harassing women or their advances are encouraged, in turn forcing women to reject men politely, only resulting in more sexual advances from men.<ref name="Goffman-1977">{{Cite journal |last=Goffman |first=Erving |date=1977 |title=The arrangement between the sexes |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00206983 |journal=Theory and Society |language=en |volume=4 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/BF00206983 |s2cid=11045745 |issn=0304-2421 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518022028/https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00206983 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Armstrong-2018"/> Through Quinn (2002) asking men to imagine themselves as women, they unintentionally revealed the harm it causes women. The men began to claim they would make sure to dress appropriately and in ways that would not draw the attention of other men, so they would not be targeted. It was this information that revealed the harm Girl Watching caused to women.<ref name="Quinn-2002a">{{Cite journal |last=Quinn |first=Beth A. |date=2002 |title=Sexual Harassment and Masculinity: The Power and Meaning of "Girl Watching" |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243202016003007 |journal=Gender & Society |language=en |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=386–402 |doi=10.1177/0891243202016003007 |s2cid=145230013 |issn=0891-2432 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518022030/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243202016003007 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Quinn continued to learn more about men's feelings towards the game and its effect on women through her interviews. Quinn learned that it was fun for men until they got caught. If a woman looked towards the group watching her during their remarks or said something to them, it would make things awkward and no longer be the fun game they were playing. This is because men were looking at women as objects, and as soon as the women made notice of them or they got caught, they would become a subject objecting, ruining their game because she was no longer an object for their enjoyment.<ref name="Quinn-2002a" /> Women are seen as objects, with no feelings or thoughts, not as subjects.<ref>{{Citation |last=Schwalbe |first=Michael L. |chapter=Social structure and the moral self |date=29 March 1991 |title=The Self-Society Dynamic |pages=281–304 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511527722.015 |isbn=978-0-521-38433-9 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/selfsociety-dynamic/social-structure-and-the-moral-self/3C854CD7905583DB3D0CC35484725576|archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518022033/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/selfsociety-dynamic/social-structure-and-the-moral-self/3C854CD7905583DB3D0CC35484725576 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
[[File:Affiche contre le harcèlement.Métro de Londres.20220404 144408.jpg|alt=Text-based ad on a red background, saying "INTRUSIVE STARING OF A SEXUAL NATURE IS SEXUAL HARASSMENT AND IS NOT TOLERATED / See it or experience it on public transport? Text what, where and when to 6106. In an emergency always dial 999. Aware of someone who is doing this and want to remain anonymous? Call the sexual harassment line on 0800 783 0137. Together, we can stop sexual harassment." Sponsored by Mayor of London, CrimeStoppers, British Transport Police, and Transport for London.|left|thumb|London public service advertisement stating that intrusive, sexual staring is sexual harassment.]]
This sexual harassment does not occur merely because of men's attraction to women, but rather as a power move. Similar to most cases of sexual harassment, men tend to harass as a way of staying in power.<ref name="Cassino-2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Cassino |first1=Dan |last2=Besen-Cassino |first2=Yasemin |date=2019 |title=Race, threat and workplace sexual harassment: The dynamics of harassment in the United States, 1997–2016 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gwao.12394 |journal=Gender, Work & Organization |language=en |volume=26 |issue=9 |pages=1221–1240 |doi=10.1111/gwao.12394 |s2cid=197738092 |issn=0968-6673|url-access=subscription }}</ref> When men feel threatened, they will resort to sexual harassment as a way of maintaining their power. Men also harass as a way of maintaining their masculinity, especially when they feel it is threatened.<ref name="Goffman-1977"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=West |first1=Candace |last2=Zimmerman |first2=Don H. |date=1987 |title=Doing Gender |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243287001002002 |journal=Gender & Society |language=en |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=125–151 |doi=10.1177/0891243287001002002 |s2cid=220519301 |issn=0891-2432 |access-date=8 May 2023 |archive-date=29 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329160146/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0891243287001002002 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> When some men feel that their masculinity or their gender are threatened, they may resort to sexual harassment as a means of reinforcing their dominance and assuring themselves of their identity. Along with this, when men felt threatened, the likelihood of their participation in sexual harassing behaviors increased.<ref name="Cassino-2019" /> There is an unequal power balance between men and women, and this is a result of sexual harassment. This power balance, being unequal, is partly rooted in the sexual harassment of women by men with a view to the perpetuation of the latter's power.<ref name="Messner-2016">{{Cite journal |last=Messner |first=Michael A. |date=2016 |title=Bad Men, Good Men, Bystanders: Who Is the Rapist? |journal=Gender & Society |language=en |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=57–66 |doi=10.1177/0891243215608781 |s2cid=147250801 |issn=0891-2432|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== In the military ===
{{Main|Sexual harassment in the military}}

Studies of sexual harassment have found that it is markedly more common in the [[military]] than in [[civilian]] settings.<ref name="British Army-2015">{{cite Individuals detained by the military are also vulnerable to sexual harassment. During the [[Iraq War]], for example, personnel of the [[United States Army|US army]] and [[Central Intelligence Agency|US Central Intelligence Agency]] committed many [[human rights violations]] against detainees in the [[Abu Ghraib prison]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.salon.com/news/abu_ghraib/2006/03/14/chapter_5/index.html|title=Chapter 5: Nov. 4–5, 2003 "Other government agencies"|last1=Scherer|first1=Michael|last2=Benjamin|first2=Mark|date=14 March 2006|editor-last=Walsh|editor-first=Joan|work=Salon.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080212035108/http://www.salon.com/news/abu_ghraib/2006/03/14/chapter_5/index.html|archive-date=12 February 2008|access-date=3 April 2012}}</ref> including [[rape]], [[sodomy]], and other forms of sexual abuse.<ref name="New Yorker 2004-05-17">{{cite news|last=Hersh|first=Seymour M.|url=http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2004/05/17/040517fa_fact2?currentPage=all|title=Chain of Command|date=10 May 2004|magazine=The New Yorker|access-date=13 September 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120101055751/http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2004/05/17/040517fa_fact2?currentPage=all|archive-date=1 January 2012|quote=NBC News later quoted U.S. military officials as saying that the unreleased photographs showed American soldiers "severely beating an Iraqi prisoner nearly to death, having sex with a female Iraqi prisoner, and 'acting inappropriately with a dead body.' Although the risk of sexual misconduct in the armed forces is widely acknowledged, personnel are frequently reluctant to report incidents, typically out of fear of reprisals, according to research in Australia, Canada, France, the UK, and the US.<ref name="British Army-2015" /><ref name="Deschamps-2015">{{Cite web|url=http://www.forces.gc.ca/assets/FORCES_Internet/docs/en/caf-community-support-services-harassment/era-final-report-(april-20-2015)-eng.pdf|title=External Review into Sexual Misconduct and Sexual Harassment in the Canadian Armed Forces|last=Deschamps|first=Marie|date=2015|website=forces.gc.ca|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180308232139/http://www.forces.gc.ca/assets/FORCES_Internet/docs/en/caf-community-support-services-harassment/era-final-report-(april-20-2015)-eng.pdf|archive-date=8 March 2018|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref><ref name="Leila-2014" /><ref name="Rutherford-2006" /><ref name="Lichfield-2014" /><ref name="Cornall-2016">{{Cite web|url=https://www.defenceabusetaskforce.gov.au/Reports/Documents/Dart-final-report-2016.pdf|title=Defence Abuse Response Taskforce: Final report|last=Defence Abuse Response Taskforce|date=March 2016|publisher=Australian Government|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180313191521/https://www.defenceabusetaskforce.gov.au/Reports/Documents/Dart-final-report-2016.pdf|archive-date=13 March 2018|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Moon Cronk|first=Terri|url=https://www.war.gov/News/News-Stories/Article/Article/1168765/dod-releases-latest-military-sexual-assault-report/|title=DoD Releases Latest Military Sexual Assault Report|date=1 May 2017|work=DOD News|access-date=9 March 2018|url-status=live|publisher=US Department of Defence|language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309182920/https://www.defense.gov/News/Article/Article/1168765/dod-releases-latest-military-sexual-assault-report/|archive-date=9 March 2018}}</ref>

Women affected by sexual harassment are more likely than other women to suffer [[Stress (biology)|stress]]-related [[Mental disorder|mental illness]] afterward.<ref name="Watkins-2018b" /> Research in the US found that when [[sexual abuse]] of female military personnel is [[Psychological trauma|psychiatrically traumatic]], the odds of suffering from [[Posttraumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD) after deployment on operations increase by a factor of nine.<ref name="Anderson-2013" />

== Measurement ==

=== Research design ===

==== Sampling techniques ====
Sampling techniques are important to all types of research. Sampling matters because it affects the generalizability of the results and how they can be used to better understand sexual harassment.{{Editorializing|date=May 2023}} Two sampling methods are probability sampling and non-probability sampling, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses for the study.<ref name="Gillespie-1987">{{Cite journal |last1=Gillespie |first1=Dair L. |last2=Leffler |first2=Ann |date=December 1987 |title=The Politics of Research Methodology in Claims-Making Activities: Social Science and Sexual Harassment |journal=Social Problems |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=490–501 |doi=10.2307/800543 |jstor=800543 |issn=0037-7791 }}</ref>

Probability sampling involves taking a sample from a subset of the population using random selection. The random selection used in probability sampling is key to making the results generalizable to the population that is being studied, which makes it more widely used than other nonrandom methods.<ref name="Gillespie-1987" /> Although the use of probability sampling has its perks, the data may not be representative or generalizable because the research is limited to certain contexts/environments. Sampling only people in a particular environment makes the results applicable only to that environment. For example, the results from a study of sexual harassment done in an office space in China cannot apply to the occurrence of sexual harassment at an American university.<ref name="Gillespie-1987" /> Similarly, if the sample being used is too small, it cannot be generalized to the larger population.

Despite its potential for bias, non-probability sampling may be used when research lacks funding or the number of available participants is small.<ref name="Gillespie-1987" /> The selection of participants in non-probability sampling is nonrandom and is often the most convenient. Many of the early studies of sexual harassment, such as the survey by the Working Women's Institute (1975) and the Redbook Survey, have relied on convenience or non-probability sampling.<ref name="Gillespie-1987" /> The sampling was often done at conventions, meetings, or sent out in letters or magazines.{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}}

===== Importance of wording =====
