In May 2002, the [[European Union]] Council and Parliament amended a 1976 Council Directive on the equal treatment of men and women in employment to prohibit sexual harassment in the workplace, naming it a form of sex discrimination and violation of dignity. This Directive required all Member States of the European Union to adopt laws on sexual harassment, or amend existing laws to comply with the Directive by October 2005.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stopvaw.org/Domestic_Legal_Framework.html?Type=B_BASIC&SEC=%7BD7FABC81-256E-41C1-BF3A-563AD89AA809%7D|title=Domestic Legal Framework|last=Stop Violence Against Women|date=13 July 2007|publisher=The Advocates for Human Rights|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116004349/http://www.stopvaw.org/Domestic_Legal_Framework.html?Type=B_BASIC&SEC=%7BD7FABC81-256E-41C1-BF3A-563AD89AA809%7D|archive-date=16 November 2018|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

In 2005, China added new provisions to the ''Law on Women's Rights Protection'' to include sexual harassment.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/4625913.stm |title=China to outlaw sexual harassment |work=BBC News |date=27 June 2005 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120730155433/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/4625913.stm |archive-date=30 July 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2006, "The Shanghai Supplement" was drafted to help further define sexual harassment in China.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Li |first1=Cao |last2=South |first2=Mark |url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2006-10/27/content_718147.htm |title=Draft bill details sexual harassment |publisher=China Daily |date=27 October 2006 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024012122/http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2006-10/27/content_718147.htm |archive-date=24 October 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Sexual harassment was specifically criminalized for the first time in modern Egyptian history in June 2014.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Hendawi|first1=Hamza|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/sexual-assault-on-student-sparks-outrage-in-egypt/|title=Sexual assault on student sparks outrage in Egypt Read more: Sexual assault on student sparks outrage in Egypt|date=10 June 2014|work=The Times of Israel|access-date=7 November 2014|url-status=live|agency=Associated Press|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141107120444/https://www.timesofisrael.com/sexual-assault-on-student-sparks-outrage-in-egypt/|archive-date=7 November 2014}}</ref>

{{As of|2016||df=}}, sexual harassment remains legal in Kuwait<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2016/country-chapters/kuwait|title=World Report 2016: Kuwait|publisher=[[Human Rights Watch]]|year=2016|chapter=Women's Rights, Sexual Orientation, and Gender Identity|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-date=5 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180605213413/https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2016/country-chapters/kuwait|url-status=live}}</ref> and Djibouti.<ref>[https://2009-2017.state.gov/documents/organization/252887.pdf "Djibouti 2015 Human Rights Report"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190907015343/https://2009-2017.state.gov/documents/organization/252887.pdf |date=7 September 2019 }}, [[United States Department of State]] [[Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor]].</ref>

===Varied legal guidelines and definitions===
'''The [[United Nations]] General Recommendation 19 to the convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women''' defines sexual harassment of women to include:

<blockquote>such unwelcome sexually determined behavior as physical contact and advances, sexually colored remarks, showing pornography and sexual demands, whether by words or actions. Such conduct can be humiliating and may constitute a health and safety problem; it is discriminatory when the woman has reasonable ground to believe that her objection would disadvantage her in connection with her employment, including recruitment or promotion, or when it creates a hostile working environment.</blockquote>

While such conduct can be harassment of women by men, many laws around the world that prohibit sexual harassment recognize that both men and women may be harassers or victims of sexual harassment. However, most claims of sexual harassment are made by women.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc/statistics/enforcement/sexual_harassment.cfm |title=Sexual Harassment Charges: EEOC & FEPAs Combined: FY 1997 – FY 2011 |publisher=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007201224/http://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc/statistics/enforcement/sexual_harassment.cfm |archive-date=7 October 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

There are many similarities and also important differences in laws and definitions used around the world.

===Africa===
====Egypt====
Sexual harassment is rife in Egypt. A 2013 study from the United Nations showed that 99.3 percent of Egyptian women have suffered some form of sexual harassment. Authorities punish women when they do speak out.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20190722-egypt-15-year-old-girl-detained-for-stabbing-her-rapist/|title=Egypt: 15-year-old girl detained for stabbing her rapist|date=22 July 2019|website=Middle East Monitor|access-date=25 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191212024928/https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20190722-egypt-15-year-old-girl-detained-for-stabbing-her-rapist/|archive-date=12 December 2019|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.albawaba.com/node/egyptians-defend-young-girl-killed-her-rapist-face-law-1298118|title=Egyptians Defend Young Girl Who Killed Her Rapist In Face of The Law|date=18 July 2019|website=Al Bawaba|access-date=25 November 2019|archive-date=13 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613105943/https://www.albawaba.com/node/egyptians-defend-young-girl-killed-her-rapist-face-law-1298118|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20191106-egypt-girl-who-stabbed-her-rapist-released/|title=Egypt girl who stabbed her rapist released|date=6 November 2019|website=Middle East Monitor|access-date=25 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191107135752/https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20191106-egypt-girl-who-stabbed-her-rapist-released/|archive-date=7 November 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Morocco====
In 2016, a stricter law proscribing sexual harassment was proposed in Morocco, specifying fines and a possible jail sentence of up to 6 months.<ref name="tmt_24March2016">{{cite news|url=http://themoroccantimes.com/2016/03/18929/sexual-harrassement-morocco-jail-sentence|title=Up to 6 Months in Jail if You Sexually Harass a Woman in Morocco|date=24 March 2016|work=The Moroccan Times|access-date=11 October 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011143631/http://themoroccantimes.com/2016/03/18929/sexual-harrassement-morocco-jail-sentence|archive-date=11 October 2016}}</ref> The existing law against harassment was reported not to be upheld, as harassment was not reported to police by victims and even when reported, was not investigated by police or prosecuted by the courts.<ref name="tmt_24March2016" /><ref name="bbc_mag_10Oct2016">{{cite news |title=The Moroccan women fighting daily sexual harassment |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-37589687 |access-date=11 October 2016 |work=BBC Magazine |publisher=[[BBC]] |date=10 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161010235625/http://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-37589687 |archive-date=10 October 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>
On 1 June 2023, a Moroccan court sentenced a 32-year-old man to two years in prison for sexually harassing and forcibly kissing a woman inside a church.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://themoroccantimes.com/2023/06/25902/man-sentenced-to-two-years-in-jail-for-sexual-harassment-and-kissing-inside-tangier-church|title=Man Sentenced to Two Years in Jail for Sexual Harassment and Kissing Inside Tangier Church|work=The Moroccan Times |date=3 June 2023|access-date=3 June 2023|archive-date=2 June 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602161339/https://themoroccantimes.com/2023/06/25902/man-sentenced-to-two-years-in-jail-for-sexual-harassment-and-kissing-inside-tangier-church|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Australia===
The [[Sex Discrimination Act 1984]] defines sexual harassment as "... a person sexually harasses another person (the person harassed ) if: (a) the person makes an unwelcome sexual advance, or an unwelcome request for sexual favours, to the person harassed; or (b) engages in other unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in relation to the person harassed; in circumstances in which a reasonable person, having regard to all the circumstances, would have anticipated the possibility that the person harassed would be offended, humiliated or intimidated".<ref>{{cite Legislation AU|Cth|act|sda1984209|Sex Discrimination Act 1984|28A}}.</ref>

===Europe===
In the [[European Union]], there is a [[Directive (European Union)|directive]] on sexual harassment. The ''Directive 2002/73/EC – equal treatment of 23 September 2002 amending Council Directive 76/207/EEC on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions'' states:<ref name="eur-lex.europa.eu" />
<blockquote>For the purposes of this Directive, the following definitions shall apply: (...)
* sexual harassment: where any form of unwanted verbal, non-verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature occurs, with the purpose or effect of violating the dignity of a person, in particular when creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment
Harassment and sexual harassment within the meaning of this Directive shall be deemed to be discrimination on the grounds of sex and therefore prohibited.</blockquote>

The [[Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence]] also addresses the issue of sexual harassment (Article 40), using a similar definition.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://conventions.coe.int/Treaty/EN/Treaties/Html/210.htm|title=Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (CETS No. 210)|last=Council of Europe|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923210455/http://www.conventions.coe.int/Treaty/EN/Treaties/Html/210.htm|archive-date=23 September 2015}}</ref>

====Denmark====
Sexual harassment is defined as any verbal, non-verbal, or physical action used to change a victim's sexual status against the will of the victim. It results in the victim feeling inferior or having their dignity hurt. Men and women are looked upon as equal, and any action trying to change the balance in status with the differences in sex as a tool is also sexual harassment. In the workplace, jokes, remarks, etc., are considered discriminatory only if the employer has stated so in their written policy. Law number 1385 of 21 December 2005 regulates this area.<ref name="Denmark law">{{cite web|url=http://www.ku.dk/regel/2/2002.html#LOV%20nr%201385|title=Denmark Law|date=29 June 2016|publisher=Københavns Universitet|language=da|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321222932/http://www.ku.dk/regel/2/2002.html#LOV%20nr%201385|archive-date=21 March 2012|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.retsinformation.dk/forms/r0710.aspx?id=137042|title=Ligebehandlingsloven – Bekendtgørelse af lov om ligebehandling af mænd og kvinder med hensyn til beskæftigelse m.v|website=www.retsinformation.dk|language=da|trans-title=The Equal Treatment Act – Executive Order on the Equal Treatment Act for men and women with regard to employment, etc.|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181214022811/https://www.retsinformation.dk/Forms/R0710.aspx?id=137042|archive-date=14 December 2018|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

====France====
In [[France]], both the Criminal Code and the Labor Code are relevant to sexual harassment. Until 4 May 2012, article 222-33 of the French Criminal Code described sexual harassment as "The fact of harassing anyone in order to obtain favors of a sexual nature".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichTexte.do?cidTexte=JORFTEXT000000408905|title=Loi n° 2002–73 du 17 janvier 2002 de modernisation sociale|date=17 January 2002|website=Legifrance|language=fr|trans-title=Art. 179 of the Law no. 2002-73 of 17 January 2002 on social modernization|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207182819/https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichTexte.do?cidTexte=JORFTEXT000000408905|archive-date=7 February 2018|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> Since 2002, the law has recognized the possibility of sexual harassment between co-workers and not only by supervisors. On 4 May 2012, the [[Constitutional Council (France)|Supreme Court of France]] quashed the definition of the criminal code as being too vague.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/en/decision/2012/2012240QPC.htm|title=Decision no. 2012-240 QPC of May 4, 2012|website=Conseil constitutionnel|language=en|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190602055255/https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/en/decision/2012/2012240QPC.htm|archive-date=2 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> The 2012 decision resulted from a law on priority preliminary rulings on the issue of constitutionality. As a consequence of this decision, all pending procedures before criminal courts were canceled. Several feminist NGOs, such as AFVT, criticized this decision. President [[François Hollande]], the Minister of Justice (Christiane Taubira), and the Minister of Equality (Najat Belkacem) asked that a new law be voted on rapidly. As a result, ''LOI n°2012-954 du 6 août 2012'' was voted in, providing a new definition.<ref>[http://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichCodeArticle.do?idArticle=LEGIARTI000021796942&cidTexte=LEGITEXT000006070719 "Code pénal: Article 222-33" (in French)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612163504/https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichCodeArticle.do?idArticle=LEGIARTI000021796942&cidTexte=LEGITEXT000006070719 |date=12 June 2018 }}, ''legifrance.gouv.fr''.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fonction-publique.gouv.fr/loi-6-aout-2012-relative-au-harcelement-sexuel|title=Loi du 6 août 2012 relative au harcèlement sexuel|date=20 September 2012|website=Le portail de la Fonction publique [The Civil Service Portal]|language=fr|trans-title=Law of August 6, 2012 on sexual harassment|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191001072531/https://www.fonction-publique.gouv.fr/loi-6-aout-2012-relative-au-harcelement-sexuel|archive-date=1 October 2019|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> In addition to criminal provisions, the French Labor code also prohibits sexual harassment.<ref>Act of 2 November 1992</ref> The legislator voted a law in 2008<ref>Act of 27 May 2008</ref> that copied the 2002/73/EC Directive<ref>Directive of 23 September 2002 amending Council Directive 76/207/EEC on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=Directive 2002/73/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2002 amending Council Directive 76/207/EEC on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions (Text with EEA relevance)|date=5 October 2002|url=http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/73/oj/eng|volume=OJ L|issue=32002L0073|language=en|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-date=18 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518023047/https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/73/oj/eng|url-status=live}}</ref> definition without modifying the French Labour Code.

According to Abigail C. Saguy in her book ''What is Sexual Harassment: From Capitol Hill to the Sorbonne'', "According to French penal law, '''sexual''' '''harassment''' is also different from rape and sexual assault in that it does not involve physical contact. Rather, with '''sexual harassment''', economic dependence and official authority alone are used to pressure a person into having sexual relations(pg.24)."

====Germany====
[[File:1833 Neder Im Gasthof anagoria.JPG|thumb|''At the Tavern'', by Johann Michael Neder, 1833, [[Germanisches Nationalmuseum]]]]
In June 2016, the governing coalition decided on the key points of a tightening of the law governing sexual offenses (Sexualstrafrecht, literally: law on the punishment of sexual delicts). On 7 July 2016, the Bundestag passed the resolution<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.spiegel.de/politik/deutschland/bundestag-beschliesst-neues-sexualstrafrecht-a-1101813.html|title=Votum: Bundestag beschließt neues Sexualstrafrecht|date=7 July 2016|journal=Spiegel Online|access-date=7 July 2016|url-status=live|language=de|trans-title=Vote: Bundestag passes new sexual criminal law|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160707120628/http://www.spiegel.de/politik/deutschland/bundestag-beschliesst-neues-sexualstrafrecht-a-1101813.html|archive-date=7 July 2016}}</ref> and by fall of that year, the draft bill will be presented to the second chamber, the Bundesrat.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.spiegel.de/politik/deutschland/sexualstrafrecht-alles-was-sie-zu-nein-heisst-nein-wissen-muessen-a-1101658.html|title=Neues Sexualstrafrecht: Nein heißt Nein. Und was bedeutet das jetzt?|date=7 July 2016|journal=Spiegel Online|access-date=7 July 2016|url-status=live|language=de|trans-title=New Sexual Criminal Law: No means No. And what does that mean now?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180120202657/http://www.spiegel.de/politik/deutschland/sexualstrafrecht-alles-was-sie-zu-nein-heisst-nein-wissen-muessen-a-1101658.html|archive-date=20 January 2018}}</ref> By this change, sexual harassment shall become punishable under the ''Sexualstrafrecht''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dw.com/de/nein-hei%C3%9Ft-nein-koalition-reformiert-sexualstrafrecht/a-19336217|title='Nein heißt Nein' – Koalition reformiert Sexualstrafrecht|date=16 June 2016|publisher=Deutsche Welle|language=de|trans-title="No means No" – coalition reforms sexual criminal law|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617135723/http://www.dw.com/de/nein-hei%C3%9Ft-nein-koalition-reformiert-sexualstrafrecht/a-19336217|archive-date=17 June 2016|access-date=18 June 2016}}</ref>

Now, sexual harassment is punishable by law according to § 184i of the law governing sexual offenses. The law only states unwanted physical contact as sexual harassment, but has been extended in 2020 to include "cybergrooming" as well.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dejure.org/gesetze/StGB/184i.html|title=Sexuelle Belästigung|access-date=10 July 2020|website=dejure.org|archive-date=7 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807025502/https://dejure.org/gesetze/StGB/184i.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Greece====
In response to the EU Directive 2002/73/EC, [[Greece]] enacted Law 3488/2006 (O.G.A. 191).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://evaw-global-database.unwomen.org/en/countries/europe/greece/2006/law-3488-2006-on-the-implementation-of-the-principle-of-equal-treatment-of-men-and-women|title=Law 3488/2006: Framework on Equal Treatment of Men and Women|website=Global Database on Violence against Women|publisher=[[United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women|UN Women]]|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-date=18 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518023104/https://data.unwomen.org/evaw/database|url-status=live}}</ref> The law specifies that sexual harassment is a form of gender-based discrimination in the workplace. Victims also have the right to compensation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId%3D10297%26baseHREF%3Dcountry%26baseHREFId%3D563|title=LAW 3488/2006 ON THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PRINCIPLE OF EQUAL TREATMENT OF MEN AND WOMEN IN THE FIELDS OF ACCESS TO EMPLOYMENT, VOCATIONAL TRAINING AND PROMOTION, TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF WORK|date=7 September 2009|website=The UN Secretary-General's database on violaence against women|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201171917/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=10297&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=563|archive-date=1 February 2014|access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref> Before this law, the policy on sexual harassment in Greece was very weak. No law defined sexual harassment, and victims could only use general laws, which were very poor in addressing the issue.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1408&context=hrbrief|title=The New European Union Directive on Sexual Harassment and Its Implications for Greece|last=Tsekos|first=Mary Ellen|date=2003|website=Human Rights Brief|publisher=Center for Human Rights & Humanitarian Law|access-date=11 February 2020|archive-date=13 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613233629/https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1408&context=hrbrief|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.intellectum.org/articles/issues/intellectum3/en/ITL03p015025_Sexual%20Harassment%20in%20the%20Greek%20Criminal%20Law_Elissavet%20Symeonidou%20Kastanidou.pdf|title=The Sexual Harassment in Greek Criminal Law (Law 3488/2006)|last=Symeonidou-Kastanidou|first=E.|date=30 May 2007|website=Intellectum|others=Translated by Victor Tsilonis and Danai Roussou|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202101821/http://www.intellectum.org/articles/issues/intellectum3/en/ITL03p015025_Sexual%20Harassment%20in%20the%20Greek%20Criminal%20Law_Elissavet%20Symeonidou%20Kastanidou.pdf|archive-date=2 February 2014|access-date=2 February 2014}}</ref>

====Russia====
As of 2023, there is no formal law in Russia that prohibits or criminalizes repeated sexual harassment or any sexual advancements that result in women or men losing their jobs or any other adverse effects that can be proven in a court of law. Per articles 132-133 of the [[Criminal Code of Russia|Criminal Code of Russian Federation]] (CC RF), only criminal sexual conduct is outlawed, including all non-consensual sex between individuals: [[rape]], sex with underage, etc. Per Article 133 (formerly Article 118 of the CC RF 1990), various forms of extortion and coercion are also criminalized.<ref name=":0" />

According to a 1997 Moscow Center for Gender Studies study, in practically all cases, authorities did not investigate or enforce these articles.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://shsf.invisionzone.com/index.php?s=a1f5e83af0f492d74310d4d1a073b792&showtopic=279|title=Sexual Harassment in Russian Workplaces|last=Khotkina|first=Dr. Zoya|date=25 April 1997|publisher=Moscow Centre for Gender Studies|via=Sexual Harassment Support Forum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311060132/http://shsf.invisionzone.com/index.php?s=a1f5e83af0f492d74310d4d1a073b792&showtopic=279|archive-date=11 March 2007}}</ref>

In 2008, ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' quoted a survey in which "100 percent of female professionals [in Russia] said they had been subjected to sexual harassment by their bosses, 32 percent said they had had intercourse with them at least once and another seven percent claimed to have been raped."<ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/russia/2470310/Sexual-harrassment-okay-as-it-ensures-humans-breed-Russian-judge-rules.html |title = Sexual harassment okay as it ensures humans breed, Russian judge rules |last = Blomfield |first = Adrian |date = 29 July 2008 |newspaper = The Daily Telegraph |access-date = 15 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110711120823/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/russia/2470310/Sexual-harrassment-okay-as-it-ensures-humans-breed-Russian-judge-rules.html |archive-date = 11 July 2011 |url-status = live }}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The current source is insufficiently reliable ([[WP:NOTRS]]).|date=January 2024}}

====Switzerland====
A ban on discrimination was included in the Federal Constitution (Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the old Federal Constitution) in 1981 and adopted in Article 8, Paragraph 2 of the revised Constitution. The ban on sexual harassment in the workplace forms part of the Federal Act on Gender Equality (GEA) of 24 March 1995, which includes several provisions prohibiting discrimination in employment and is intended to promote equality. Article 4 of the GEA defines the circumstances, Article 5 sets out legal rights, and Article 10 protects against dismissal during the complaints procedure.<ref name="Swiss.gov-2017">{{cite web|url=https://www.admin.ch/opc/en/classified-compilation/19950082/index.html|title=Federal Act on Gender Equality|date=1 January 2017|website=The Federal Council – The Portal of the Swiss Government|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180324102217/https://www.admin.ch/opc/en/classified-compilation/19950082/index.html|archive-date=24 March 2018|access-date=23 March 2018}}</ref> Article 328, paragraph 1 of the Code of Obligations (OR), Article 198 (2) of the Penal Code (StGB) and Article 6, paragraph 1 of the Employment Act (ArG) contain further statutory provisions on the ban on sexual harassment. The ban on sexual harassment is intended exclusively for employers, within the scope of their responsibility for protecting legal personality, mental and physical well-being, and health.{{citation needed|date=January 2014}}

Article 4 of the GEA of 1995 discusses the topic of sexual harassment in the workplace: "Any harassing behaviour of a sexual nature or other behaviour related to the person's sex that adversely affects the dignity of women or men in the workplace is discriminatory. Such behaviour includes in particular threats, the promise of advantages, the use of coercion and the exertion of pressure in order to obtain favours of a sexual nature."<ref name="Swiss.gov-2017" />

====United Kingdom====
The Discrimination Act of 1975 was amended in 1986 to establish sexual harassment as a form of discrimination.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eoc-law.org.uk/default.aspx?page=4666|title=Strathclyde Regional Council v Porcelli [1986&#93; IRLR 134 Court of Session|work=Equal Opportunities Commission|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080408051338/http://www.eoc-law.org.uk/default.aspx?page=4666|archive-date=8 April 2008}}</ref> It states that harassment occurs where there is unwanted conduct on the ground of a person's sex or unwanted conduct of a sexual nature and that conduct has the purpose or effect of violating a person's dignity, or of creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for them. If an employer treats someone less favorably because they have rejected, or submitted to, either form of harassment described above, this is also harassment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eoc.org.uk/Default.aspx?page=15657|title=Sexual Harassment: what the law says|date=10 August 2010|website=Equal Opportunities Commission|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070831002533/http://www.eoc.org.uk/Default.aspx?page=15657|archive-date=31 August 2007|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref> In March 2021, a study by UN Women UK found that 97% of young women aged 18–24 have experienced some sexual harassment.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 March 2021 |title=Four-fifths of young women in the UK have been sexually harassed, survey finds |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/mar/10/almost-all-young-women-in-the-uk-have-been-sexually-harassed-survey-finds |access-date=30 December 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518023044/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/mar/10/almost-all-young-women-in-the-uk-have-been-sexually-harassed-survey-finds |url-status=live }}</ref>

Sexual harassment is also now considered discrimination under [[Equality Act 2010|the Equality Act 2010.]] The Equality Act 2010 consolidated over 116 separate pieces of legislation into a single act that protects citizens' rights and promotes equality for all.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en/equality-act-2010/what-equality-act|title=What is the Equality Act?|publisher=Equality and Human Rights Commission|website=www.equalityhumanrights.com|access-date=8 April 2020|archive-date=20 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200320021852/https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en/equality-act-2010/what-equality-act}}</ref> The new law strengthened the protection of individuals from discrimination in some areas. It is designed to protect individuals from discrimination based on age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. It covers a wide range of areas, including employment, education, housing, public accommodations, and the provision of goods and services. Under the Equality Act 2010, it is unlawful to discriminate against someone based on any of these protected characteristics. This includes direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, harassment, and victimization. The Act also imposes a duty on public authorities, such as local councils and government departments, to consider the impact of their policies and decisions on people with protected characteristics, and to take steps to promote equality of opportunity and eliminate discrimination.<ref>Maria Khan, and Ayesha Ahmed, "The protection against harassment of women at the workplace act 2010: A legislative review." ''Lahore University of Management Sciences law Journal'' 3 (2016): 91+  [https://scholar.archive.org/work/os3iqu54obhdxblxehylrico5q/access/wayback/https://sahsol.lums.edu.pk/sites/default/files/harassment_of_women.pdf online].</ref>

Although the 2010 Equality Act is in place, many are pushing the UK government to put even more policies in place to stop sexual harassment in the workplace. One group in particular, "This is Not Working", acts because, according to recent surveys done by the Women and Equalities Committee, workplace sexual harassment is still very prevalent, even with the current legislation. The movement pushes for even more employers to take responsibility and proactively prevent sexual harassment.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.natlawreview.com/article/not-working-answer-one-consultation-please-uk|title=This is Not Working – the Answer? One Consultation, Please (UK)|website=The National Law Review|language=en|access-date=12 April 2020|archive-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200614105311/https://www.natlawreview.com/article/not-working-answer-one-consultation-please-uk|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Asia ===
==== China ====
In [[China]], the 2005 Law for the Protection of Women's Rights and Interests of the People's Republic of China states "sexual harassment against women is prohibited"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cecc.gov/resources/legal-provisions/protection-of-womens-rights-and-interests-law-of-the-peoples-republic-of|title=Protection of Women's Rights and Interests Law of the People's Republic of China (Chinese and English Text)|website=Congressional-Executive Commission on China|date=28 August 2005 |url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418130448/https://www.cecc.gov/resources/legal-provisions/protection-of-womens-rights-and-interests-law-of-the-peoples-republic-of|archive-date=18 April 2019|access-date=18 April 2019}}</ref> although the law does not explicitly define what sexual harassment is.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shrm.org/resourcesandtools/legal-and-compliance/employment-law/pages/global-china-anti-harassment-requirements.aspx|title=China: Time to Review Your Policies Against Sexual Harassment|last1=Ligorner|first1=K. Lesli|last2=Wang|first2=Dora|date=24 August 2018|website=SHRM|language=en-US|access-date=18 April 2019|archive-date=18 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418130446/https://www.shrm.org/resourcesandtools/legal-and-compliance/employment-law/pages/global-china-anti-harassment-requirements.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

Sexual harassment is still pervasive within Chinese culture. A 2018 survey of female journalists revealed that 80% had experienced unwanted behavior,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/society/article/2142703/why-chinese-women-dont-speak-out-about-sexual-harassment|title=Why sexual harassment in the workplace goes unreported in China|last=Zuo|first=Mandy|date=21 April 2018|website=South China Morning Post|language=en|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418130448/https://www.scmp.com/news/china/society/article/2142703/why-chinese-women-dont-speak-out-about-sexual-harassment|archive-date=18 April 2019|access-date=18 April 2019}}</ref> and an online survey of college students from all 34 [[Provinces of China|provinces]] the same year revealed that 75% of female students and 35% of male students had experienced sexual harassment.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ucanews.com/news/sexual-harassment-common-on-chinese-campuses/82604|title=Sexual harassment common on Chinese campuses|date=20 June 2018|website=UCA News|language=en|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418130448/https://www.ucanews.com/news/sexual-harassment-common-on-chinese-campuses/82604|archive-date=18 April 2019|access-date=18 April 2019}}</ref>

==== Lebanon ====
As of 2020, it is estimated that one in four women in [[Lebanon]] have been subjected to some form of unsolicited sexual advance, ranging from verbal to physical.<ref name="Yassine-2020">{{Cite web|last=Yassine|first=Hussein|date=21 December 2020|title=Lebanese Parliament Just Voted To Criminalize Sexual Harassment|url=https://www.the961.com/lebanese-parliament-sexual-harassment/|access-date=21 December 2020|website=The961|language=en-US|archive-date=21 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221120026/https://www.the961.com/lebanese-parliament-sexual-harassment/|url-status=live}}</ref> On 21 December 2020, the [[Parliament of Lebanon|Lebanese Parliament]] passed a law criminalizing sexual harassment.<ref name="Yassine-2020" /> There was no national legislation to directly criminalize sexual harassment before this, with draft laws being proposed several times without effect.<ref name="Yassine-2020" />

====India====
{{Further|Sexism in India|Eve teasing|The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013}}

Sexual harassment in [[India]] is termed "[[Eve teasing]]" and is described as: unwelcome sexual gesture or behavior, whether directly or indirectly as sexually colored remarks; physical contact and advances; showing pornography; a demand or request for sexual favours; any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct being sexual in nature or passing sexually offensive and unacceptable remarks. The critical factor is the unwelcomeness of the behavior, which makes the impact on the recipient more relevant than the perpetrator's intent.<ref name="india_rape" /> According to the [[Indian constitution]], sexual harassment infringes the fundamental right of a woman to gender equality under Article 14 and her right to life and live with dignity under Article 21.<ref name="amicus.iupindia.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.amicus.iupindia.org/Lels_WorkplaceHarassment_ovw.asp|title=ICFAI University – Workplace Harassment|website=Amicus.iupindia.org|url-status=usurped|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171202183755/http://www.amicus.iupindia.org/Lels_WorkplaceHarassment_ovw.asp|archive-date=2 December 2017|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref><!-- The archives are only of the domain reselling page -->

In 1997, the [[Supreme Court of India]], in a [[Public Interest Litigation]], defined sexual harassment at the workplace, preventive measures, and a redress mechanism. The judgment is popularly known as Vishaka Judgment.<ref name="Vishaka 001">{{cite journal |url = http://indiankanoon.org/doc/1031794/ |title = Vishaka & Ors vs State Of Rajasthan & Ors on 13 August 1997 |author1=Manohar, SV |author2=Kirpal, BN |journal=Supreme Court of India  |date=August 1997 |volume=241 |id = SCC Ref:(1997)6. SCC 241 : (1997 AIR SCW 3043) |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120605101608/http://indiankanoon.org/doc/1031794/ |archive-date=5 June 2012 }}</ref> In April 2013, India enacted its own law on sexual harassment in the workplace—[[The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013]]. Almost 16 years after the Supreme Court's landmark guidelines on preventing sexual harassment in the workplace (known as the "[[Vishaka Guidelines]]"), the Act has endorsed many of them. It is a step towards codifying gender equality. The Act is intended to cover all women employees, including those in the unorganized sector and domestic workers. The Indian law does not permit the victim or complainant to take assistance of a legal professional in the inquiry, however, in Arti Devi Vs Jawaharlal Nehru University,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://indiankanoon.org/doc/195150471/|title=The Redressal of Public Grievances Rules, 1998|work=Indian Kanoon|access-date=28 February 2020|archive-date=28 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200228064147/https://indiankanoon.org/doc/195150471/|url-status=live}}</ref> the High Court of Delhi permitted the complainant to avail the services of a counsel as her defence assistant.

The Act has identified sexual harassment as a violation of the fundamental rights of a woman to equality under articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India and her right to life and to live with dignity under article 21 of the Constitution; as well as the right to practice any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business which includes a right to a safe environment free from sexual harassment. The Act also states that protection against sexual harassment and the right to work with dignity are universally recognized human rights under international conventions and instruments, such as the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against Women, which the Government of India ratified on 25 June 1993.<ref>[[The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013]]</ref>{{Circular reference|date=February 2020}}

The [[Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013]] introduced changes to the [[Indian Penal Code]], making sexual harassment an express offense under Section 354A, punishable with imprisonment for up to 3 years and/or a fine. The Amendment also introduced new sections making acts like disrobing a woman without consent, stalking, and sexual acts by a person in authority an offense.

====Israel====
The 1998 Israeli Sexual Harassment Law interprets sexual harassment broadly. It prohibits the behavior as a discriminatory practice, a restriction of liberty, an offense to human dignity, a violation of every person's right to elementary respect, and an infringement of the right to privacy. Additionally, the law prohibits intimidation or retaliation thus related to sexual harassment are defined by the law as "prejudicial treatment".<ref name="Kamir">{{cite journal | last1 = Kamir | first1 = Orit | title = Israel's 1998 Sexual Harassment Law: Prohibiting Sexual Harassment, Sexual Stalking, and Degradation Based on Sexual Orientation in the Workplace and in all Social Settings | url = http://sitemaker.umich.edu/Orit_Kamir/files/sexharas2.pdf | journal = International Journal of Discrimination and the Law | volume = 2005 | issue = 7 | pages = 315–336 | access-date = 7 October 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151017132743/http://sitemaker.umich.edu/Orit_Kamir/files/sexharas2.pdf | archive-date = 17 October 2015 }}</ref>

====Japan====
{{main|Sexual harassment in Japan}}
[[File:Chikan Sign.jpg|301x301px|thumb|SexPublic sign in [[Chiba, Chiba|Chiba, Japan]], warning of [[Chikan (body contact)|''chikan'']]]]

The Department of Labor received 11,289 consultations regarding sexual harassment (approximately 60% from female workers, 5% from male workers, and 35% from others) in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gender.go.jp/about_danjo/whitepaper/h27/zentai/html/zuhyo/zuhyo01-04-14.html |title=都道府県労働局雇用均等室に寄せられた職場におけるセクシュアル・ハラスメントの相談件数 |publisher=内閣府 |language=ja |access-date=3 August 2022 |archive-date=6 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230306235221/https://www.gender.go.jp/about_danjo/whitepaper/h27/zentai/html/zuhyo/zuhyo01-04-14.html |url-status=live }}</ref> However, given the generally low rate of reported sexual offenders (about 10%), the [[Dark figure of crime|dark figure]] of sexual harassers is believed to be substantial, with 34.7% of full-time employees experiencing sexual harassment, according to the Japan Institute for Labor Policy and Training.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://apj.aidem.co.jp/current/detail/1352.html |title=妊娠等を理由とする不利益取扱い及びセクシュアルハラスメントに関する実態調査 |publisher=労働政策研究・研修機構 |language=ja |access-date=3 August 2022 |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518023046/https://apj.aidem.co.jp/current/detail/1352.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

It appeared most dramatically in Japanese discourse in 1989, when a court case in Fukuoka ruled in favor of a woman who had been subjected to the spreading of sexual rumors by a co-worker. When the case was first reported, it spawned a flurry of public interest: 10 books were published, including English-language feminist guidebooks to 'how not to harass women' texts for men.<ref name="Huen">{{cite journal |last1=Huen|first1 = Y. |title=Workplace Sexual Harassment in Japan: A Review of Combating Measures Taken |journal=Asian Survey |year=2007|volume=47|issue=5|pages=811–827 |doi = 10.1525/as.2007.47.5.811 }}</ref> Sekuhara was named 1989's 'Word of the Year'. The case was resolved in the victim's favor in 1992, awarding her about $13,000 in damages, the first sexual harassment lawsuit in Japanese history.<ref name="MacGregor">{{cite news |last = MacGregor |first = Hillary |title = In Japan, Many Men Just Don't Get It: Nation only got word for sexual harassment after '89 court case. |url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-10-13-mn-56533-story.html |newspaper = Los Angeles Times |access-date = 26 October 2015 |date = 13 October 1995 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160105082011/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-10-13/news/mn-56533_1_sexual-harassment/2 |archive-date = 5 January 2016 |url-status = live }}</ref> Laws then established two forms of sexual harassment: ''taika-gata'', in which rewards or penalties are explicitly linked to sexual acts, and ''kankyo-gata'', in which the environment is made unpleasant through sexual talk or jokes, touching, or hanging sexually explicit posters.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/koyou_roudou/koyoukintou/seisaku06/index.html#h2_free5 |title=職場におけるセクシュアルハラスメントについて |publisher=厚生労働省 |language=ja |access-date=3 August 2022 |archive-date=2 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802222316/https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/koyou_roudou/koyoukintou/seisaku06/index.html#h2_free5 |url-status=live }}</ref> This applies to everyone in an office, including customers.<ref name="Huen" />

====Malaysia====
{{main|Sexual harassment in Malaysia}}

In Malaysia, sexual harassment as defined by the [http://www.agc.gov.my/agcportal/uploads/files/Publications/LOM/EN/Act%20265%20-%20Employment%20Act%201955.pdf Employment Act 1955] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111235552/http://www.agc.gov.my/agcportal/uploads/files/Publications/LOM/EN/Act%20265%20-%20Employment%20Act%201955.pdf |date=11 November 2020 }}, is "any unwanted conduct of a sexual nature, whether verbal, non-verbal, visual, gestural or physical, directed at a person which is offensive, humiliating or a threat to their well-being". The Act does not distinguish between males and females or between employers and employees. As such, sexual harassment can be committed by a female against a male, or an employee against an employer.

Sexual harassment is common, and since 2010, trains on the Malaysian Railway have included pink-colored [[women-only passenger car|women-only cars]] as a means of cutting down on it.<ref name="buses">{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna40468372|title=Women-only buses aim to halt sex harassment|work=NBC News|date=2 December 2010|access-date=9 June 2017|archive-date=21 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201021054650/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/40468372/ns/world_news-asia_pacific/t/women-only-buses-aim-halt-sex-harassment/|url-status=live}}</ref> There are also women-only buses in Kuala Lumpur since 2010.<ref name="buses" /> In 2011, the government launched a women-only taxi service in the greater Kuala Lumpur area.<ref name="taxis">{{cite web|url=http://www.alarabiya.net/articles/2011/11/27/179417.html|title=Malaysia launches women-only taxis, hoping to reduce number of rape and robbery cases|work=Agence France-Presse|publisher=Al Arabiya News|date=27 November 2011|access-date=9 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171004034930/http://www.alarabiya.net/articles/2011/11/27/179417.html|archive-date=4 October 2017}}</ref> The taxis have women drivers, and operate on an on-call basis.<ref name="taxis" />

==== New Zealand ====
In 2018, Statistics New Zealand published the findings of the Survey of Working Life, which queried employed individuals about their work schedules, employment circumstances, and levels of job satisfaction and work-life balance. 9% of males and 14% of women reported having dealt with bullying, harassment, or discrimination at work in the preceding year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Continued reports of sexual harassment, assault and bullying at work; steps towards change {{!}} New Zealand Family Violence Clearinghouse |url=https://nzfvc.org.nz/news/continued-reports-sexual-harassment-assault-and-bullying-work-steps-towards-change |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=nzfvc.org.nz |archive-date=20 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020130128/https://nzfvc.org.nz/news/continued-reports-sexual-harassment-assault-and-bullying-work-steps-towards-change |url-status=live }}</ref> Any invitation for sexual activity, whether direct or indirect, is considered sexual harassment according to the Employment Relations Act of 2000.  The individual harassing the victim may be a boss, an employee, a volunteer, a coworker, an employer's representative, or even a customer, contractor, or supplier who is not an employee.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is sexual harassment |url=https://www.employment.govt.nz/resolving-problems/types-of-problems/bullying-harassment-and-discrimination/sexual-harassment/what-is-sexual-harassment/ |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=Employment New Zealand |language=en-NZ |archive-date=20 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020132734/https://www.employment.govt.nz/resolving-problems/types-of-problems/bullying-harassment-and-discrimination/sexual-harassment/what-is-sexual-harassment/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, the duties of PCBU (person undertaking a business or undertaking) are according to the act 36, subpart 2, Duties of PCBU are

·       "The provision and maintenance of a work environment that is without risks to health and safety"; and

·       "The provision and maintenance of safe plant and structures"; and

·       "The provision and maintenance of safe systems of work"; and

·       "The safe use, handling, and storage of plants, substances, and structures".<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Zealand legislation |url=https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2015/0070/latest/DLM5976894.html#DLM5976894 |access-date=30 September 2023 |archive-date=12 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812161708/https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2015/0070/latest/DLM5976894.html#DLM5976894 |url-status=live }}</ref>

As per the Employment Relations Act 2000, you can file a personal grievance. A worker may file a personal grievance against their employer. You have 12 months from the date when the assault happened or became aware of your knowledge, whichever comes first.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Steps for workers to address sexual harassment |url=https://www.employment.govt.nz/resolving-problems/types-of-problems/bullying-harassment-and-discrimination/sexual-harassment/steps-for-workers-to-address-sexual-harassment/ |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=Employment New Zealand |language=en-NZ |archive-date=20 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020212630/https://www.employment.govt.nz/resolving-problems/types-of-problems/bullying-harassment-and-discrimination/sexual-harassment/steps-for-workers-to-address-sexual-harassment/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Employment Relations (Extended Time for Personal Grievance for Sexual Harassment) Amendment Act 2023 and, section 54 amended states, an explanation in simple terms of the resources that are available for resolving issues with relationships at work, in relation to the 12-month period that must pass before filing a personal grievance under section 114(1) if the grievance relates to sexual harassment under section 103(1)(d).<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Zealand Legislation |url=https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2023/0028/latest/LMS577477.html |website=New Zealand Legislation |access-date=30 September 2023 |archive-date=1 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230701094045/https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2023/0028/latest/LMS577477.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Human Rights Act 1993 under 62 sexual harassment states that, in the course of engaging in any of the activities covered by the provisions of subsection (3), it is illegal for anyone to ask another person for sexual relations, sexual contact, or any other type of sexual activity when doing so contains an implicit or overt guarantee of favorable treatment. During one's engagement in each of the areas where subsection (3) applies, it is forbidden for an individual to subject another individual to the conduct of the actions that follow:

(a) a conduct that is unwanted or offensive to that individual (regardless of whether that is communicated to the first-mentioned individual); and

(b) an act that is either repeated or of a significant nature as to negatively impact that individual in relation to any of the regions where subsection (3) applies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Human rights act 1993 |url=https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1993/0082/latest/DLM304651.html |website=New Zealand Legislation |access-date=30 September 2023 |archive-date=15 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240215200435/https://legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1993/0082/latest/DLM304651.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Pakistan ====
Pakistan introduced the [[Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010|''Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act'']] in 2010. This law defines the act of harassment as. "[A]ny unwelcome sexual advance, request for sexual favors or other verbal or written communication or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitude, causing interference with work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile or offensive work environment, or the attempt to punish the complainant for refusal to such a request or is made a condition for employment".

The Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010, was the first legislative measure in South Asia specifically enacted to address sexual harassment in professional environments. The Act was designed, drafted, and advocated by the civil society network AASHA ([[Alliance Against Sexual Harassment]], which played a central role in its development. Simultaneously, a companion amendment to Section 509 of the Pakistan Penal Code (Act XLV 1860)<ref>{{Cite web |title=THE PAKISTAN PENAL CODE |url=https://pakistancode.gov.pk/pdffiles/administratord5622ea3f15bfa00b17d2cf7770a8434.pdf}}</ref> and the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Act V of 1898) Section 509 was passed and signed. While the Protection Act established internal mechanisms within organizations for the review and resolution of harassment complaintants' sexual harassment law,<ref>{{Cite web |title=understanding pakistan' sexual harassment law |url=https://tribune.com.pk/article/90571/understanding-pakistans-sexual-harassment-law-part-1  https://tribune.com.pk/article/91190/understanding-pakistans-sexual-harassment-law-part-ii}}</ref> the Penal Code amendment extended the scope of legal recourse by allowing individuals to file harassment complaints nationwide, mandating police registration of such cases.

Following presidential assent on 8 March 2010, Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani constituted the ''National Implementation Watch Committee'' <sup>[1]</sup> to oversee the enforcement of the Act. Dr. [[Fouzia Saeed]], a founding member of AASHA, was appointed Chairperson of the committee.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aziz |first=Farieha |title=Interview: Dr Fouzia Saeed, National Implementation Watch Committee |url=https://newslinemagazine.com/magazine/interview-dr-fouzia-saeed-national-implementation-watch-committee/ |access-date=4 October 2025 |website=Newsline |language=en}}</ref> The implementation rules were formally published in The Gazette of Pakistan<ref>{{Citation |title=The Gazette of Pakistan |date=14 September 2025 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Gazette_of_Pakistan&oldid=1311320169 |access-date=4 October 2025 |language=en}}</ref> on 15 January 2011, marking the beginning of nationwide enforcement.

The legislative process leading to the enactment of the Act spanned a decade and has been documented extensively.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saeed |first=Fouzia |title=The AASHA Experience: A Decade of Struggle Against Sexual Harassment in Pakistan |publisher=Mehergarh Research and Publications |year=2011 |isbn=978-969-9659-07-2}}</ref> Subsequent efforts to amend the Act, both successful and unsuccessful, have also been recorded.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saeed |first=Fouzia |title=On Their Own Terms: Early 21st Century Women's Movements in Pakistan |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2020 |isbn=978-0-19-070259-5 |location=Karachi, Pakistan}}</ref> A comprehensive review of the Act's implementation over the following ten years was published by Mehergarh, authored by Maliha Husain, highlighting both achievements and ongoing challenges.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Husain |first=Maliha |title=An Objective Analysis of Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010 |publisher=Mehergarh Research and Publications |year=2022 |location=Islamabad, Pakistan}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Husain |first=Maliha |title=A Game Changer for Women: Reviewing Ten Years of Implementing the Anti-Sexual Harassment Laws in Pakistan, 2010–2020 |publisher=Mehergarh Research and Publications |year=2020 |isbn=978-969-9659-13-3 |location=Islamabad, Pakistan}}</ref>

====Philippines====
The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act of 1995 was enacted:<ref>{{cite web |url = http://filipiniana.net/read_content.jsp?filename=L00000000018 |title = Republic Act No. 7877 Anti Sexual Harassment Act of 1995 |website = Filipiniana.net |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url = https://archive.today/20120713063240/http://filipiniana.net/read_content.jsp?filename=L00000000018 |archive-date=13 July 2012 }}</ref>

<blockquote>primarily to protect and respect the dignity of workers, employees, and applicants for employment as well as students in educational institutions or training centers. This law, consisting of ten sections, provides for a clear definition of work, education or training-related sexual harassment and specifies the acts constituting sexual harassment. It likewise provides for the duties and liabilities of the employer in cases of sexual harassment, and sets penalties for violations of its provisions. A victim of sexual harassment is not barred from filing a separate and independent action for damages and other relief aside from filing the charge for sexual harassment.</blockquote>

Assistant Solicitor General Derek Puertollano was dismissed from service over 3 administrative charges for violations of RA 7877, "The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act of 1995", filed by a complaint from his legal interns. He was convicted of the grave offense of sexual harassment through unwanted touching of the private part of the body, and the less grave offenses of sexual harassment through unwanted touching or brushing against a victim's body, and through surreptitiously looking at a person's private part. "These harrowing incidents left complainants traumatized, scarring them both for life," said [[Lucas Bersamin]] in his decision dated 20 February 2024. [[Menardo Guevarra]] appointed an OIC to the vacated legal division.<ref>{{cite news |last1= Buan |first1= Lian|title=Malacañang fires assistant solicitor general for sexual harassment|url= https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/inside-track/malacanang-fires-assistant-solicitor-general-for-sexual-harassment/|access-date=27 February 2024 |publisher= [[Rappler]]|date=27 February 2024}}</ref>

===United States===
====Evolution of sexual harassment law====
=====Workplace=====
{{main|Sexual harassment in the workplace in the United States}}

In the United States, the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]] prohibits [[employment discrimination]] based on [[Race (classification of human beings)|race]], [[Biological sex|sex]], [[color]], [[national origin]] or [[religion]]. {{UnitedStatesCode|42|2000e-2}} was initially intended only to combat sexual harassment of women, but the prohibition on [[sex discrimination]] covers both men and women. This discrimination occurs when the sex of the worker is made a condition of employment (i.e., all female waitpersons or male carpenters) or where this is a job requirement that does not mention sex but ends up preventing many more persons of one sex than the other from the job (such as height and weight limits). This act only applies to employers with 15 or more employees.<ref name="EEOC-2018">{{Cite web |title=Sexual Harassment |url=https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/types/sexual_harassment.cfm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180308120009/https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/types/sexual_harassment.cfm |archive-date=8 March 2018 |access-date=11 February 2020 |website=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission}}</ref>

''[[Barnes v. Train]]'' (1974) is commonly viewed as the first sexual harassment case in America, even though the term "sexual harassment" was not used.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wendymcelroy.com/ifeminists/2004/1027.html|title=The Sad Evolution of Sexual Harassment|last=McElroy|first=Wendy|date=27 October 2004|website=ifeminists.com|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807125033/http://www.wendymcelroy.com/ifeminists/2004/1027.html|archive-date=7 August 2011|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> In 1976, ''Williams v. Saxbe'' established sexual harassment as a form of sex discrimination when sexual advances by a male supervisor towards a female employee, if proven, would be deemed an artificial barrier to employment placed before one gender and not another. In 1980, the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]] (EEOC) issued regulations defining sexual harassment and stating it was a form of sex discrimination prohibited by the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In the 1986 case of ''[[Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson]]'', the Supreme Court first recognized "sexual harassment" as a violation of Title VII, established the standards for analyzing whether the conduct was welcome; levels of employer [[legal liability|liability]], and that speech or conduct in itself can create a "[[hostile environment sexual harassment|hostile environment]]".<ref>{{caselaw source |case=''Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson'', 477 U.S. 57 (1986) |findlaw=http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?navby=CASE&court=US&vol=477&page=57|internetarchive={{IA SCOTUS URL |id=micro_IA40385012_0940}}|justia=http://supreme.justia.com/us/477/57/case.html}}</ref> This case filed by Mechelle Vinson ruled that the sexual conduct between the subordinate and supervisor could not be deemed voluntary due to the hierarchical relationship between the two positions in the workplace.<ref>{{Cite book |title = Women and the law stories |year=2011|publisher=Foundation Press/Thomson Reuters |last1= Schneider |first1 = Elizabeth M. |last2 = Wildman |first2 = Stephanie M. |isbn = 978-1-59941-589-5 |location=New York, NY |oclc = 671639786 }}</ref> Following the ruling in ''[[Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson]]'', reported sexual harassment cases grew from 10 cases being registered by the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|EEOC]] per year before 1986 to 624 case being reported in the subsequent following year.<ref name="Cochran-2004">{{cite book |title=Sexual harassment and the law: the Mechelle Vinson case |last=Cochran |first=Augustus B. |year=2004 |publisher=University Press of Kansas |isbn=978-0-7006-1323-6 |location=Lawrence, KS |oclc=53284947 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/sexualharassment0000coch }}</ref> This number of reported cases to the EEOC rose to 2,217 in 1990 and then 4,626 by 1995.<ref name="Cochran-2004" />

The [[Civil Rights Act of 1991]] added provisions to Title VII protections including expanding the rights of women to sue and collect compensatory and punitive [[damages]] for sexual discrimination or harassment; the case of ''Ellison v. Brady'' (US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit – 924 F.2d 872 (9th Cir. 1991)) resulted in rejecting the [[reasonable person]] standard in favor of the "reasonable woman standard" which allowed for cases to be analyzed from the perspective of the complainant and not the defendant.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://shsf.invisionzone.com/index.php?showtopic%3D445 |title=Sexual Harassment Support Forum |access-date=19 July 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070310223845/http://shsf.invisionzone.com/index.php?showtopic=445 |archive-date=10 March 2007 }}{{full citation needed|date=December 2013}}</ref> However, some legal scholars have argued this does not go far enough and that the reasonable person standard also needs to take [[intersectionality]] into account.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Onwuachi-Willig |first1=Angela |author-link=Angela Onwuachi-Willig |title=What About #UsToo?: The Invisibility of Race in the #MeToo Movement |journal=Yale Law Journal Forum |date=18 June 2018 |volume=128 |page=109 |url=https://scholarship.law.bu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1331&context=faculty_scholarship |access-date=10 February 2020 |archive-date=21 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200221161738/https://scholarship.law.bu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1331&context=faculty_scholarship |url-status=live }}</ref> Also in 1991, ''[[Jenson v. Eveleth Taconite Co.]]'' became the first sexual harassment case to be given [[class action]] status paving the way for others. Seven years later, in 1998, through that same case, new precedents were established that increased the limits on the "[[Discovery (law)|discovery]]" process in sexual harassment cases, which then allowed psychological injuries from the [[litigation]] process to be included in assessing damages awards. In the same year, the courts concluded in ''Faragher v. City of Boca Raton, Florida'', and ''[[Burlington v. Ellerth]]'', that employers are liable for harassment by their employees.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=us&vol=000&invol=97-282 |title=U.S Supreme Court: Beth Ann Faragher, petitioner v. City of Boca Raton |work=FindLaw |date=26 June 1998 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110624090220/http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=us&vol=000&invol=97-282 |archive-date=24 June 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=us&vol=000&invol=97-569 |title = U.S. Supreme Court: Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth |work = FindLaw |date = 26 June 1998 |access-date = 7 October 2012 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110624090225/http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=us&vol=000&invol=97-569 |archive-date = 24 June 2011 |url-status = live }}</ref> Moreover, ''[[Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services]]'' set the precedent for same-sex harassment, and sexual harassment without motivation of "sexual desire", stating that any discrimination based on sex is actionable so long as it places the victim in an objectively disadvantageous working condition, regardless of the gender of either the victim, or the harasser.

In the 2006 case of ''[[Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. White]]'', the standard for retaliation against a sexual harassment complainant was revised to include any adverse employment decision or treatment that would be likely to dissuade a "reasonable worker" from making or supporting a charge of discrimination.

During 2007 alone, the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and related state agencies received 12,510 new charges of sexual harassment on the job.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Marshall |first1=David  |last2=Andronici |first2 = Justine |title=Sexual Harassment Law: A Brief Introduction for New Practitioners |url = http://www.kmblegal.com/index.php/160/Sexual_Harassment_Law_A_Brief_Introduction_for_New_Practitioners |publisher=Katz, Marshall & Banks |access-date=18 March 2011|date=23 October 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090203063912/http://www.kmblegal.com/index.php/160/Sexual_Harassment_Law_A_Brief_Introduction_for_New_Practitioners |archive-date=3 February 2009 }}</ref> In ''Astra USA v. Bildman'', 914 N.E.2d 36 (Mass. 2009), applying New York's [[faithless servant]] doctrine, the court held that a company's employee who had engaged in financial misdeeds and sexual harassment must "forfeit all of his salary and bonuses for the period of disloyalty".<ref name="auto6x">{{cite book |url = https://books.google.com/books?id=3RaGDwAAQBAJ&q=%22faithless+servant%22&pg=PA472|title=Employment Law: Private Ordering and Its Limitations |first1=Timothy P. |last1=Glynn |first2=Rachel S.|last2=Arnow-Richman |first3=Charles A. |last3=Sullivan |year = 2019 |publisher=Wolters Kluwer Law & Business |via=Google Books |isbn=978-1-5438-0106-4 }}</ref> The court held that this was the case even if the employee "otherwise performed valuable services", and that the employee was not entitled to recover restitution for the value of those other services.<ref name="auto6x" /><ref>{{cite journal |title=Faithless Servants Beware: Massachusetts Forfeiture Law is More Severe than Astra USA, Inc. v. Bildman Might Suggest |first1=James R.|last1=Carroll|first2=Jason Collins|last2=Weida|journal=Boston Bar Journal |issue = Winter 2010 |date=1 January 2010 |ssrn = 1775205}}</ref>

The 2010 case, ''[[Reeves v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.]]'' ruled that a hostile work environment can be created in a workplace where sexually explicit language and [[pornography]] are present. A [[hostile workplace]] may exist even if it is not targeted at any particular employee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.employmentlawblog.info/2010/01/reeves-v-ch-robinson-worldwide-inc-no-07-10270-11th-cir-jan-20-2010.shtml|title=Reeves v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc., No. 07-10270 (11th Cir. Jan. 20, 2010)|last=Mollica|first=Paul|date=19 January 2010|website=Employment Law Blog|publisher=Outten & Golden LLP|language=en-US|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160521135648/http://www.employmentlawblog.info/2010/01/reeves-v-ch-robinson-worldwide-inc-no-07-10270-11th-cir-jan-20-2010.shtml|archive-date=21 May 2016|access-date=17 June 2016}}</ref>

From 2010 through 2016, approximately 17% of sexual harassment complaints filed with the EEOC were made by men.<ref>{{cite web|title=Charges Alleging Sex-Based Harassment (Charges filed with EEOC) FY 2010 – FY 2016|url=https://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc/statistics/enforcement/sexual_harassment_new.cfm|website=Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|access-date=15 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815232935/https://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc/statistics/enforcement/sexual_harassment_new.cfm|archive-date=15 August 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>

=====Education=====
{{Main|Sexual harassment in education in the United States}}

[[Title IX]] of the Education Amendments of 1972 (United States) states, "No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance."

In ''[[Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools]]'' (1992), the U.S. Supreme Court held that private citizens could collect damage awards when teachers sexually harassed their students.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/503/60 |title=Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools |publisher=Legal Information Institute |date=26 February 1992 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025214756/http://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/historics/USSC_CR_0503_0060_ZS.html |archive-date=25 October 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> In ''[[Bethel School District No. 403 v. Fraser]]'' (1986), the courts ruled that schools have the power to discipline students if they use "obscene, profane language or gestures" which could be viewed as substantially interfering with the educational process, and inconsistent with the "fundamental values of public school education".<ref>{{cite web |first = Doug |last = Linder |url = http://law2.umkc.edu/faculty/projects/ftrials/firstamendment/bethel.html |title = Bethel School District v. Fraser |website = Law.umkc.edu |access-date = 7 October 2012 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120927043125/http://law2.umkc.edu/faculty/projects/ftrials/firstamendment/bethel.html |archive-date = 27 September 2012 |url-status = live }}</ref> Under regulations issued in 1997 by the U.S. [[United States Department of Education|Department of Education]], which administers [[Title IX]], school districts should be held responsible for harassment by educators if the harasser "was aided in carrying out the sexual harassment of students by his or her position of authority with the institution".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/docs/sexhar00.html|title=Sexual Harassment Guidance|date=13 March 1997|website=Office for Civil Rights|publisher=U.S. Department of Education|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120919234735/http://www2.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/docs/sexhar00.html|archive-date=19 September 2012|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref> In ''Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education'', and ''Murrell v. School Dist. No. 1'', 1999, schools were assigned liability for peer-to-peer sexual harassment if the plaintiff sufficiently demonstrated that the administration's response showed "deliberate indifference" to "actual knowledge" of discrimination.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=US&vol=000&invol=97-843 |title=Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education |work=FindLaw |date=24 May 1999 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024014255/http://caselaw.lp.findlaw.com/scripts/getcase.pl?court=US&vol=000&invol=97-843 |archive-date=24 October 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-10th-circuit/1261260.html|title=MURRELL v. ACLU IX|last=United States Court of Appeals, Tenth Circuit.|date=4 August 1999|website=FindLaw|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320050213/http://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-10th-circuit/1261260.html|archive-date=20 March 2016|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

====Additionally====
There are some legal options for a complainant in the U.S.: [[mediation]], filing with the EEOC or filing a claim under a [[U.S. state|state]] Fair Employment Practices (FEP) statute (both are for workplace sexual harassment), filing a common law [[tort]], etc.<ref name="whattodo">{{cite web|url=http://www.feminist.org/911/harasswhatdo.html|title=Sexual Harassment Fact Sheet: What to Do if You or Someone You Know is Sexually Harassed|date=2014|publisher=Feminist Majority Foundation|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020062451/http://www.feminist.org/911/harasswhatdo.html|archive-date=20 October 2012|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref> Not all sexual harassment will be considered severe enough to form the basis for a legal claim. However, most often, several types of harassing behavior are present, and there is no minimum level of harassing conduct under the law.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> The section below "EEOC Definition" describes the legal definitions that have been created for sexual harassment in the workplace. Definitions similar to the EEOC definition have been created for academic environments in the U.S. Department of Education Sexual Harassment Guidance.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/docs/shguide.html |title=Revised Sexual Harassment Guidance |publisher=Office for Civil Rights, U.S. Department of Education |date=19 January 2001 |access-date=7 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120919234743/http://www2.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/docs/shguide.html |archive-date=19 September 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====EEOC Definition====
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission claims that it is unlawful to harass an applicant or employee of any sex in the workplace. The harassment could include sexual harassment. The EEOC says that the victim and harasser could be any gender and that the other does not have to be of the opposite sex. The law does not ban offhand comments, simple teasing, or minor incidents. If the harassment reaches the point of creating a hostile work environment, it will be addressed.<ref name="eeoc"/> In 1980, the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]] produced a set of guidelines for defining and enforcing Title VII (in 1984 it was expanded to include educational institutions). The EEOC defines sexual harassment as:

Unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, or other verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature when:

# Submission to such conduct was made either explicitly or implicitly a term or condition of an individual's employment,
# Submission to or rejection of such conduct by an individual was used as the basis for employment decisions affecting such individual, or
# Such conduct has the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering with an individual's work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment.

Types 1 and 2 are called "[[quid pro quo]]" (Latin for "this for that" or "something for something"). They are essentially "sexual bribery", or the promise of benefits, and "sexual coercion".

Type 3, known as "[[hostile work environment]]", is by far the most common form. This form is less clear-cut and is more subjective.<ref name="webcom" />

'''Note:''' A workplace harassment complainant ''must'' file with the EEOC and receive a "right to sue" clearance, before they can file a lawsuit against a company in federal court.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

=====''Quid pro quo'' sexual harassment=====
[[File:Stop à la violence sexiste au travail.jpg|thumb|right|[[International Trade Union Confederation]] (2015–2017)]]

Quid pro quo means "this for that". In the workplace, this occurs when a job benefit is directly tied to an employee submitting to unwelcome sexual advances. For example, a supervisor promises an employee a raise if he or she will go out on a date with him or her, or tells an employee he or she will be fired if he or she does not sleep with him or her.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abanet.org/publiced/practical/sexualharassment_quidproquo.html|title=The Law & Your Job: What is quid pro quo harassment?|date=18 March 2013|publisher=American Bar Association|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090209001311/http://www.abanet.org/publiced/practical/sexualharassment_quidproquo.html|archive-date=9 February 2009|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref> Quid pro quo harassment also occurs when an employee makes an evaluative decision, or provides or withholds professional opportunities based on another employee's submission to verbal, nonverbal, or physical conduct of a sexual nature. Quid pro quo harassment is equally unlawful whether the victim resists and suffers the threatened harm or submits and thus avoids it.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sexualharassmentsupport.org/SHworkplace.html|title=Sexual Harassment in the Workplace|website=Sexual Harassment Support|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100402083730/http://www.sexualharassmentsupport.org/SHworkplace.html|archive-date=2 April 2010}}</ref>

===== Hostile environment sexual harassment=====
{{Main|Hostile work environment}}

This occurs when an employee is subjected to comments of a sexual nature, unwelcome physical contact, or offensive sexual materials as a regular part of the work environment. For the most part, a single isolated incident will not be enough to prove hostile environment harassment unless it involves extremely outrageous and egregious conduct. The courts will try to decide whether the conduct is both "serious" and "frequent". Supervisors, managers, co-workers, and even customers can be responsible for creating a hostile environment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abanet.org/publiced/practical/sexualharassment_hostileenvironment.html|title=The Law & Your Job: What is hostile environment harassment?|date=18 March 2013|publisher=American Bar Association|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090802171805/http://www.abanet.org/publiced/practical/sexualharassment_hostileenvironment.html|archive-date=2 August 2009|access-date=7 October 2012}}</ref>

The line between "[[quid pro quo]]" and "hostile environment" harassment is not always clear, and the two forms of harassment often occur together. For example, an employee's job conditions are affected when a sexually hostile work environment results in constructive discharge. At the same time, a supervisor who makes sexual advances toward a subordinate employee may communicate an implicit threat to retaliate against her if she does not comply.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eeoc.gov/policy/docs/currentissues.html|title=Policy Guidance on Current Issues of Sexual Harassment|date=19 March 1990|publisher=U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190910004803/https://www.eeoc.gov/policy/docs/currentissues.html|archive-date=10 September 2019|access-date=12 February 2020}}</ref>
